LADIES' LETTER.

MY DEAR NELLIE, The fashions have varied so much for leafy June that it is impossible to predict what will be the set one. In the way of headgear large shapes in pale. blue, pink, mauve, or green straws are bent about in a fashion that would almost give an air of pretti- ness to the plainest face, and trimmed with large soft ribbon bows and many flowers. A hat much to the fore is bent down on to the hair at the back, and well shades the face in front. It looks its best trimmed with trails of roses and black ribbon bows. Whether the summer will prove a propitious ore for the dainty muslins and flowery delaines that await us in such profusion remains to be seen. The last month, with its cold winds, favoured dresses of warmer material and substantial wraps, rather than the chiffon boas and neck ruffles, which appeal so much to the feminine mind.

Appearances seem to show that panne, much of it painted, in applique work is one of the favourite trimmings. The colours are very soft and bright, and, being sparingly used, the panne becomes highly effective. On an evening coat of very fine and supple-faced cloth, which I have just seen, in a shade between grey and fawn, there is an em- broidery composed of sections cut out of brightest blue and amber and crimson panne, with a little dull green in it. These are all embroidered round in chain stitch and otherwise ornamented with dull green chenille and white silk. Panne is applied in the same way to the decoration of evening gowns. Laid on net and shaped into a floral design, the panne, in yellow, rose, or pink, has, I think, a beautiful appearance, especially when the inter- vening net is kept as light and open as possible, so as to give value to the soft brightness of the panne-

A lady I met yesterday afternoon was wearing a handsome blouse of soft cherry-coloured satin. It -was tucked all over the bodice and sleeves, and had a pointed yoke back and front of creamy guipure lace insertion, and a collar-band of the same, with points standing out on either side. The hat was of black straw, trimmed with rosettes of black tulle, edged with black ribbon velvet. On the left side there were some black ostrich feathers, and at the back, under the brim, rosettes of tulle and bows of black ribbon velvet.

I saw the other day a lovely foulard walking dress, trimmed with narrow ribbon velvet. The long polonaise is bordered with the velvet, and the bodice, also edged with three rows of it, is very prettily draped across. The deep folded belt is in a dull green silk, and the bow of velvet at the neck is also green, the foulard being blue with a little foliage green intermingled with the two. The yoke and undersleeves are gathered chiffon. The very pretty hat, which a friend of mine is wearing, is in white crinoline straw, quite trans- parent, and, in colour, not unlike a thin sheet of glass. Feathers trim the upper part, and flowers are tucked uoder the brim, just above the left ear,-

A very suitable colour for a new coat is tea-rose, the latest name for mushroom, and much yellower than that hue. The trimming of it brings into play any amount of originality, though it is correct to leave the contour of the wrap in order to show that it is somewhat of a sack, though not altogether shapeless. Two laces superimposed one on the other border it most richly, and there is a still newer and more exotic adornment made of lace touched with gold braiding, mousseline choux and gold tassels. A few sprigged muslin frocks may be seen accom- panied by the new very long-tailed brocade bodice which fits the figure closely at the back and sides, but is cut in bolero form and high over the hips to descend in sash-like ends behind. White muslin insertioned with lace looks fresh and acceptable. I am of opinion that a great number of lace dresses will be seen this year, sonic of them over muslin, others over 'silk and satin. Printed mus- lins in flowered designs will be in favour, and can- vas is being made up into pretty gowns. Stone colour, beige and fawn, with butter colour and putty shades, are made over checked shot silks, and the watering in the canvas comes out very prettily over these. A thin grey canvas over a gold and white shot silk has a lovely effect. The skirt is quite untrimmed, like most of the newest. There is not much fulness at the back of the skirt near the waist, but plenty round the hem, where the silk lining is finished with half-a-dozen little rippling frills.
Your loving,
JENNIE.

The famous Wallace collection at Hertford House, Manchester Square, which was visited the other day by the Prince anu Princess of Wales and other members of the Royal Family, is now accessible to the public. There is little to add to what has already been written atout these priceless objects of art.which were mainly bre tight together by the third and fourth Marquises of Hertford, and by the late SA. Richard Wallace, to whom they were bequeathed. But N souse respects such as the (iisplay of arms and armour, of seventeenth and eighteenth cen- tury furniture. and Sevres porcelain, and in certain schools of painting, the collection is unequalled in Europ?, aid it makes a notable addition to the Art Galleries of the Metropolis and of the nation. As is well- hnown, it was left to the country by Lady Wallace,who was a French woman on her death in 1897. One of the conditions of the bequest was that a special museum mould be built for the collection, but this was over- ruhd, and Hertford House itself was purchased and enlarged, and the collection le-arranged for public ex. hibition. The Wallace Collection is, by a long way, the most magnificent gilt ever left by a private donor to the nation. Many of its treasures are beyond nrire, and it is doubtful it the estimated £6,000,000 or £7,000.000 re- presents the full monetary value of the collection. There are some prople however, who will scarcely appreciate this generous gift to the public. The Earl of Yarmouth for instance, the son of the present Marquis of Hertford. and to whom in the ordinary way the collect ing might have been expected to descend, has recently explained his affairs in the Bankruptes Court, when he stated that he finds £3OO a year" insufficient for his wants." Like Lord Rosslyn, when other things failed, the Earl turned to the stage as a pr,fes=ion, and it is hardly to be expected that he will share the general satisfaction at the bestowal of the Wallace Collection upon the nation: Whisperer of Lady Rsndolph Churchill's eneagement to Captain Cornwallis-Weat of the Seots Guards, have long been current,and her second marriage will occasion no surprise in society circles. She is, of course. an Xmerican by birth, formerly Miss Jennie Jerome of New Ynik, and married Lord Randolph Churchill in 1874. Captain Cornwallis West is much the younger of the two, being ia fact a year senior to Mr Winston Churchill Lady Randolph's eldest SOD. When the war broke out Captain Cornwallis-West left for South Africa, with Colonel Paget, but was very shortly invalided home. This was before Lady Randolph arrived out, in the hospital ship "Maine," and it was a joke that the Captain only narrowly escaped being removed from the field of danger by "Maine "force. It is understood that when Mr Winston Churchill returns from South Africa, he will write his father's life clearing up some of the shadows which overclouded the last year of that brilliant states- men's short career. " The misery that need not be" was the aubject of a lecture at the Wemen's Institute the other day, by Madame Sarah Grand, the authoress of the " Heavenly" Twins." She is not satisfied with human nature, and it seems doubtful whether there ever was anrone who has b en. Lady Warwick for instance recently stated that "she would give anything in ;the world to be a man, but she never heard of a man " who wished he was a woman." Lady Warwick went on to complain that men did not realise their opportunities for well doing Madame Grand sa.a s precisely the same thing anew: e omen, and the worst of it is, all this fault finding with human natere does very little to alter it. There were however many good points in Sarah Grand's lecture. Discussing the hundred and one domestic miseries of our own familiar acquaintance. she said that many there need not be were due to bad cooking. That is quite true.and taking the general run of domestic troubles, many coulel. be avoided or made harmless, by asking ourselves whether they are not in the category of thove that "need not be." The most unhappy people after all says Madame Grand.ate those of wealth and leisure, of empty and purposeless 'ire,, and this should at least tend to make the non-effluent classes more contented with their lot. The Early Rising Association, which holds a Midsum- mer-mere:hie meeting in London every rear, declares that the difference between getting up at five instead of seven in the morning, is equivalent to the addition of ten rears of life, to a person of forty or fifty. Of course, if all that is said of the merits of early rising was true, there would be many more millionaires than there are, besides whole communities of centenarians and phil- osophers. In the country most people get up with the break of day, but our statesmen and great men only go to bed as a rule in the early hours of the mornine Nevertheless, few will dispute the great advantages of early rising, especially if they have to make their own way in life. Even if they are themselvez, unable to resist the temptation for the morning Slumb^r; they would often be glad to see the principles of early using more appreciated by the household domestics. Talking of early rising reminds one how many people are invariably cross and diFa7rreable the first thing in the morning. One can understand this in folks who sit up late at night over their little indulgences, but it is frequently just the ssme in those who never do any- thing of the kind. It is so, even with children. 90Me of whom always wake up cross and fretful, while others are as cheery as possible. It seems to be all a question of tomponament, and in POMP families where conven- tional amiatility is at a discount in the morning, it is not a bad rule to insist upon "no cenversation " at I breakfast either for aduls or children.

div.head: LYMM RATEPAYERS PROTEST.
div.p: LYMM RATEPAYERS PROTEST.
The Council's Proposed Expenditure.

A meeting of ratepayers of Lymm was held at the Parochial Schools on Monday evening "P 0 further con- sider the proposed large .expenditure of the Urban District Council upon the new Cauccil Chambers, Canal Bridge and Steam Fire Engine, estimated to cost £5,282 all of which it is considered mar be carried out in such a manner as to meet the requirements of Lymm at a vary reduced criat, and to pass resolutions therein." Mr. Alfred Watkin presided,and amon`g those present were— Metter. Henry Greenall (Warrington), •A W Calleroaer, I H Evans (hon. secretary, William Bayley.' W P Mackendrick,J A Thcirrasop,Thomas Ardern, W C Moore, J Rowson, John Hatton and Cbarleß Cowper, Mr, Watkin said this was not his meeting, nor bad he any personal feeling against the Lymm Urban District Council as a body, or any member of that body. They had met in the schools ',rime time beck and passed resolutions against the proposed extrava- gant expenditure of the Council and agreed that nothing should be done until proper hospital provision had been made. They had received a most generous offer ol land from Mr. Littleton Dewburst as a site for a Proposed hospital, and Mr. Pewhurst having given that land he thought that the District Council would have applied their money for the purpose of a hospital. hut they bad not done so. lhs canal bridge, he thought, ought to be made wider and stronger, but he thought £1,350 was too much to be spent on it. With regard to the Proposed steam fire engine Mr Peter Rylands had said at the last meeting, that from his exrerience a manual entrine wculd meet all the requirements of a Place like Lymm. As to the proposed new District Council buildings there could be no isoubt that to spend £3,387 on Council offices was a sheer waste of money. (Applause). Re did not !mow that even the District Oouncil were so very unanimous in this matter and so anxiona to see this large building erected. The sum of .21,500 should he ample for the purpose of any accom moraation that the District Council could wiih for. Bat I if the sum was large or small it made little difference to I him as a ratepayer. What he looked at was the Principle of the thing. Wily spend the money on Csuncil buildings? Why not spend it on a hospital ? Mr. Cnarles Cowper moved "That this meeting of ratepayers of Lsonm desires to record its strong prote.t against the proposed extravagant expenditure of tl e District Council of Lymm (for Conncil Chambers, £3,387; new iron bridge °Ye, canal, £1,350 ; steam fire engine, £5OO ; fire e•capo. £45; total £5,282), fee'ing convinced that all the requiged needs of I...rnrn and dis- trict may be met at. very considerably Las cost." As a ratepayer of Lymm he felt that it was out of all reason to spend this large sum of money on such elaberate buildings. The iron bridge certainly did want something doing to it to make it safe. He knew of no building. in Lymm where the use of a fire- escape was needed. He objected strongly to the large item of expenditure for buildinas, and if the present chambers were not large enough for the members of the Council he had no donhp that other gentlemen could be found to take (hi jr places. Mr. John Hatton, in seconding the rerolution, said he was against the spending of money on a miniature Town Hall. If they had to build let them do somethi for the present generatier, and let the future look alter itself.
The resolution was carrieci with one dis-entiant. A letter was real from Mr. Thomas Davies objectine: the scheme.

div.head: TE D.' – R , I 9 JUNE 29 1900
div.p: TE D.' - R , I 9 JUNE 29 1900

muminea artietec in which they did not believe, that they went from vile debauchery to the churches to say Masses. That from the ropes downward, the clergy were Pagan and impure. That the pardon of sins had been degraded into a trade, that a tariff for the forgiveness of sin was fixed—so much for murder, so much for lying, so much for stealing, so much for adultery. Money could buy almost anything. He shewed how the people were at the mercy of the priests, how they governed almost every office. He read extracts from historians shewing that if men dared to oppcse the priests they were excommunicated, and when that was done, it was a sin to give them shelter, a sin to give them food or help in any way, and that if anyone shewed kindness to an excom- municated person he or she was liable to the same penalty. • It was a terrible picture which he drew, and all the more terrible because every statement was sub- stantiated by a recognised historian. Before he had finished it a look of revengeful hatred settled on the faces of one part of the audience, while on the faces of the other part a look of wonderment was expressed. They had no idea of what had existed at the end of the fifteenth century. "So much for the pretty fairy tales. the pathetic picture Father Sheen has drawn of the Church prior to the Reformation," said Duncan, as he finished this part of his address. . .

The remark relieved the intense excitement, to which the audience had been -worked up, and a great laugh rose from the audience. This moment's interval allowed Duncan time to turn round and open one or two other books. In doing so he saw Alizon Neville. All the joyous triumph had gone from her eyes, her face was pale to the lips, her hands were clenched nervously. He saw, too, that Ffither Sheen's oheeks were flabby, and that he was sorely uncomfortable. .

He then sketched the immediate cause of Luther's actions. He described Tetzel's visit to the quiet German town, gave quotations from his sermons, quotations which promised that, for a sum of money, he would forgive not only the sins they had committed, but those which they intended to commit. He read the blaspllemous words of Tetzel, where he said that God no longer reigned, but that all power was given to the Pope. _ _
At this juncture the chaiiinan rung the bell. This indicated that he had only three minutes more.

"Very well," said Duncan, ."I have not at present time to deal with the supposed evil results of the Reformation, but I shall have an oppor- tunity presently. Up to the present I have shewn you the- value of Father Sheen's arguments. Argmnents, " he repeated, with a smile, "arguments —why, a boy of seven could play at ninepins with them." • ••

The homely figure appealed to the humour of the audience, and the place echoed with great laughter, and before it subsided it was time for Father Sheen to commence his second address. The old man did his best: He reiterated what he had before said; but he had lost his power over the audience. It is true the Catholic portion of the audience still cheered him, but there was no hope, no confidence in the cheer. He tried to traverse the young man's statements, but even his own friends saw that he failed. The old ,priest felt it too, and he began to be confused. He saw the good-humoured ridicule which was expressed on the people's faces, and then he did what astrue debater would never have done—he descended to invective. When his half-hour was up he had not helped his cause; thus it was that when Duncan rose the second time he was met with tumultuous cheering. lie could not help being elated; it was not in human nature to feel otherwise. He looked again at Alizon Neville's face and saw chagrin, dis- comfiture, anger. Lady Neville looked at him superciliously, scornfully, while a low growl of anger was heard in the hall. All this aroused his defiance, and caused him to speak more strongly than he had intended.

First of all he took the statements contained in Father Sheen's second address, and held them up to ridicule. Then he dealt with the indictment which the priest had hurled at Protestantism. "Look at it," the old priest had said, "look at Protestantism. Think of what it has done. It has torn the Church in pieces, it has wrecked the faith of millions, it has sent untold multitudes to eternal perdition. Look at your Protestant countries. Where is your unity? It does not exist. You are a rope of sand. You are torn to pieces by conflicting sects. Protestantism is doomed because it rests on a false foundation."

This gave Duncan the chance he had hoped for, and he used the chance to advantage. He shewed how, while Protestant countries had prospered, had become strong and mighry, Catholic countries had become weaker and weaker. He described the relative positions of Germany and Spain, and shewed that while the Pope had cursed the former and blessed the latter, the former had prospered, while the latter was crumbling into decay and was day by day becoming more impotent. He shewed that Austria and Portugal could not be said to belong to the advancing countries of the wqrld, but were becoming more and more mere names on a map. He portrayed the condition of France, largely a nation of atheists, governed by the pas- sions of the mob, a nation where justice seemed a far-off dream. He pointed out that Italy, the home of the Vatican, had only become a great nation by throwing off allegiance to the Pope, and that ever since Papacy had sulked because of the position of the Italian Government. Then he traced the history of England from the time of the Spanish Armada. He described how the Pope had blessed this movement of Spain, and cursed the heresy which had robbed him of England, - and then traced the growth of England, who, through her independence of, and freedom from priestly tyranny, the nation had marched on to greatness. He shewed how the one spot on the United Kingdom where abject povet ty and ignorance reigned was in Catholic Ireland, while Protestant Ireland was _prosETrous and contented._

"Now,'" he said, in conclusion, "have I proved my case? Was the Reformation a necessity? And have the results of the Reformation justified the action of those who freed us from Papal chains ? " When Father Sheen rose for the third time the debate was as; good as closed. Even Alizon Neville and her mother saw that it was an unequal contest. They saw that much more could be said on their side than it had come to Father Sheen's mind to say. Even the most intelligent Protestants saw that the Catholic arguments had not been ably set forth. Whatever might be the merits of the case itself, the old priest was no match for the eager young debater fresh front his studies. It was like an old worn-out soldier, who had never been at his best a good fencer, doing battle with an antiquated, rusty sword against a skilled fencer, who was young, strong, and active, and whose blade was new and bright and keen. Had one of the skilled Jesuit debaters taken the place of Father Sheen, Duncan's work would have been far more difficult; as it was he was victorious all along the line. He had estimated the Lan- cashire character, had appealed to their sturdy independence, and given the bare strong facts which they so touch love. Thus it was when he rose for his last address, he had little to answer. And for half an hour, moved to intense passion by the enthusiasm of the crowd, he poured forth a glowing tribute to the men who, he said, had made us as a nation, strong, and great, and free. With anecdote, pathos. passion, humour, he carried the audience with him, until, as he sat down, the great mass of men and women rose to their feet and gave him an ovation. • "By Jove," said a young lawyer who had come to the hall, not because be had any great interest in the subject, but because he loved a battle of brains, "Duncan has used poor old Sheen as a brush with which he has swept the floor. The fellow ought to have been a barrister." _ _ _ _
Duncan -watched while Lady Neville and Alizon left the platform, followed by the old priest. Neither of them spoke to him, but when they reached the door Alizon gave him a look which he never forgot.

Old katlhy Bray climbed on the platform and shook hands \With the young minister. "I know'd thou wert middlin' well off for brains, 'nester," he said, "but am did'n think tha 'ed so mich grit in thee." A. number of people who had gathered around laughed at the old weaver's words. And nan ta,k' a bit of advice," continued the old man. "Theo slip ant at th' side dooar, and go whoam in a cab. Ther'll ne'er be a love of free spaich while th' priests 'ave owt to do." "I'll take that advice," said Duncan. "Aye, an' a few on us will go wi"im," said another, "for tiler's a lot ov Irish aatside." "Yi, and tak' care o' thysen till this debate is ovver," continued Matthy.. Duncan Rutland realised the wisdom of this advice before a week had passed away.
CHAPTER VI.
ALIZON NEV/LLE'S DILEMMA.
During the next few days the chief topic of con- versation was the debate between Father Sheen

AIM .uunean _mamba. Never betore had the town been so moved. General election speeches seemed tame compared with addresses on Church history. At the mills, where hundreds of men and women vthered together, Father Sheen's failure was dird cussed and laughed at. The Catholics longed tr invite one of their acknowledged propagandists to meet Duncan, but they dared not do so. For, first of all, the debate was announced to be between Father Sheen and the young minister; and second, it would seem a slight on the old man to suggest it to him. The daily conversation, however, fanned the excitement into a greater flame, and hundreds secretly resolved to be 'at the Industrial Hall on the following week hours before the time announced for the commencement of the discussion. "Ther'll be nowt left o' Sheen but his gaan by th' end o' th' next fight," said one sturdy Puritan to a devoted Catholic;"th' owd man sud a know' d better nor tackle a lad like Rutland." "Wait a bit," replied the Catholic, "the gaame 's noan played aat yet. Thou'lt see that Rutland is "rukbut a gassy coward." The listeners laughed, but some did not like the tone in which the man spoke. As for Father Sheen he was never seen in the town. What he did no one knew, except that he locked himself in his study, and that no one was allowed to interrupt him. The speeches were reported verbatim in the Lynford Observer,- and Alizon Neville read them through carefully. "I hate him, mother," she said, when she had finished. "It's very unfortunate," replied Lady Neville. "I ought to have known better. It is all my fault, I am afraid."

"Why? " asked Alizon. "Well, it was I, or rather it was you, who persuaded Father Sheen to give those addresses. And it was they which caused young Rutland to challenge him. "Yes, yes, I know; but I thought that--" "Yes, I know, Alizon ; but Father Sheen is neither a scholer nor a debater. I ought to have realised that at the time. It is true his first speech was good, but I did not imagine that the young minister was so clever."

"Clever! Do you think him clever ? " "I'm afraid we can't help thinking so, darling. No one could fail to see that Father Sheen fared badly." "1 don't think him clever a bit," said Alizon, Dassionately. "He is just a vulgar, conceited—' ahe hesitated for a word—"coxcomb," she added presently "He may be all that," replied Lady Neville, "but he is none the less clever. I cannot help dreading the next meeting. I hear that many Catholics have been sorely unsettled by what was said by Mr. Duncan. No doubt he could be easily answered, and had Father Sheen been a scholar and a thinker, he would be answered; but unfortunately he is not." Alizon was silent. Up to the time when Father Sheen had met Duncan she would have contested her mother's closing statement. To her the old man had always given evidence of wide reading and sound thinking; since then, however, she had seen her mistake.

"I suppose the debate must take its course ? " she said presently. "It cannot be helped. It has been publicly announced. The hall has been engaged and the people will be there. Many Catholics will be there too, and the next subject is more dangerous than the last."
"The Infallibility of the Pope, isn't it?" "Yes."

.a. •a• "There is no doubt about it, mother, is there?" asked Alizon, anxiously. "Of course not, since the Church has decreed that it shall be an article of faith. As you know, Cardinal Newman opposed the Vatican decrees as long as he could, but when it was once decided he, of course, accepted." "Yes," replied Alizon, dubiously. Even to her it seemed strange that any body of men could decide as to whether a doctrine should be accepted by the whole Catholic world; but no doubt it was right. "And if that young man succeeds next Tuesday, as he did last Tuesday, it will be a still more dangerous blow for the Church." Lady Neville nodded. "Oh," cried the girl, eagerly, "I wish something would happen to prevent him from being there. Why does not God interfere? " "Perhaps He will, my.darling." Alizon went much among the poor Catholics of the town, and was much beloved by them. During her visits the chief topic was still the debate. Many uncomplimentary remarks were passed about Duncan, and many threats of vengeance uttered. The ignorant and unreasoning part of the people felt that they would be doing God service by pre- venting the next meeting. "Tell tha what, Miss Alizon," said one brawny man of Irish origin, but who had been brought up in the town, "yon chap is nobbut the tool of the devil." _ _
"I am afraid he is," was Alizon's unguarded
reply. "And aw believe it would be pleasin' the blessed Virgin if he war traited as th' tool o' th' -

The young girl's eyes flashed. She was terribly angry with Rutland, and she was afraid lest her old Father Confessor should again fare badly at his hands. Moreover, her Church seemed to be in danger. In the past-the Popes had passed edicts to destroy those who were enemies to the fold. She had been sometimes ashamed. to confess this, but now she saw reason for it. "Father Sheen's noan a match for yon chap," went on the man, "and there's allus a sight o' waik-kneed chaps as can't stand agin a felly wots got th' gift o' th' gab like yen. I've 'eerd o' several as 'awe said they're noan goin' to Confession agenn." " It's terrible," said Alizon. "Oh, Ido wish that he might be away somewhere next Tuesday, and miss his train, or something of that sort." The collier's eyes lit up with an angry light. "Maybe summatt'll 'appen, Miss Alizon," he said ; "let's 'oap so." "Yes, let's hope so," replied the girl. She did not realise what she was saving, and had no idea of the effect of her words on the passionate, unthinking man. When Duncan got back to his lodgings on this particular day, it was past five o'clock in the evening. He sat down to the tea which his land- lady had prepared, and was about to look over his notes before going to the Industrial Hail, when Mrs. Nutter entered, and said a lad wanted to see him. "Who is he? " asked Duncan. 'Oo ses 'oo goas to Tudor School,' replied Mrs. Nutter. _ _
Duncan went to the door, and saw a lad about fifteen years of age. "Fayther's deein', an' oo wants to si tha," said the lad. "and

"Who is your father? " asked Duncan, who are you ? " "Aw'm Bob o' th' Croft Farm's lad. They ca' me Billy Scott. Aw goa to Tudor Sunday-schoo'." "What's the matter with your father ? " "Tha doctor's geein"im up. Aw know nowt no more. Oo wants to see tha reight bad. Oo's bin a bad 'un, too." "Won't to-morrow morning do ? " "Noa. Doctor ses oo'll dee to-neet." "Where is Croft Farm ? "

"Just aboon Boggart's Clough." Duncan looked at his watch. There was just time for him to visit the man before the debate. After all, the walk might do him good ; besides, he could not think of neglecting a dying man. He told his landlady where he was going, and putting his notes in his pocket, started for Croft Farm.

"Some men will call here about a quarter-past seven, Mrs. Nutter," he said. "Will you give them these books, and tell them where I've gone ? " "Yi," said the woman, laconically. That same afternoon Alizon Neville was visiting lmong the poor Catholics of the town. It was --q,ther depressing to her that so many of her fellow- retigionists were so poor and thriftless. She could not help seeing the difference between them and the respectable working-class audience she had seen on the only occasion on which she had entered a Protestant church. As on the previous occasion, the chief subject of conversation was about the debate.
" 'Appen yo'll be there agean, Miss Alizon," said one.
"Oh, yes, I shall be there." "Ther'll be some rare fun to-neet," said the woman, mysteriously. "Fun ? " queried Alizon. "To me it is not a matter of fun."
"But, yo' knaw ? " "Know what ? " "Yo knaw as aft Rutland 'll neer turn up." "Not be there. Why ? " "You've 'eerd ? "
I"No, I've heard nothing "—all the same, her heart beat high with hope. Would her prayers be answered, after all?
"xi, °MAI wur yo as started it!" "I! What do you mean, Mrs. Pickup?" "Bridget Kelly told me all abaat it,, said tbilv woman, confidentially. _ _

"All about what?" "What yo' said to her Shan." "I said nothing particular to Shan Kelly." "But yo' did, Miss Alizon," said the WOMB* "Think agean." "I said nothing, except that it would be blessing if something prevented Mr. Rutland fron2 attending the meeting to-night." "Yi, thet's it. Weel, Shan took the hint." "What do you mean?" "He tell'd thee, didn't 'a?"

"No, nothing." "Well," said the woman, "Itutland'll noan bt theer. .00'11 be sent for to see a man wot's deein at Croft Farm, aboon Boggart's Clough." "And is there a man dying there ? " "Not as I know on," and the woman laughed. "Oo'll be on his way there by naa." "And what then?" "When oo:geets to Boggart's Clough, oo'l ge,% no further to-neet."

"But why ? " asked Alizon. excitedly. " 'Cause Shan Kelly, and aar Neil, and Bill 9 Suttle, uot works at Sutcliffe Mill, and some moor, 'll noan let him." • The plot was plain, even to Ali,zon's bewildered mind. She realised the effect of her words; she saw to what length her foolish statement might lead. _ _ _ _

"But they'll not hurt him?" she gasped. , "Noan over mich. Oo'll seem to 'ave bin suppia more nor's gooid for him—that's all," and the woman laughed. "This is terrible, terrible. Mrs. Pickup," she cried. "It is base ;it is cowardly." "Nay, nay," said the woman. with a touch of anger in her voice. "Why, it wur yo' as set Shall Kelly on." Alizon left the cottage with her head in a whirl. She saw herself a party to a brutal plot., and she walked along the gloomy street like one demented._

At first a-feeliné of jOy-possessed her. Duncatt Rutland would not be at the Industrial Hall that night. This .would mean a great triumph for Father Sheen and his party. Father Sheen would, be there, but no opponent to meet him. Con-- sequently the Cathblic faith would triuMph. Bu 6 this was only for a moment. She felt ashamed that any unthinking words of her's shduld lead tir: such base actions. Moreover, the truth might 13resent1y come out, and then, guiltless as she was,! i;she would become a by-word for every Protestant; Gin the town. But thiS was.not all, nor the worst.' The cowardliness of the act haunted her. • What could she do?
Nothing. Things must take their course., Probably the plot 'would fail. Rutland was a clever man, and he would discover the meaning of it. it would be best, therefore, that she should co nothing.

She heard the clocks of the town chiming tl' half-hour. She looked at her watch: it was half - past five. A few seconds later there was a great rattle of clogs on the stony pavements, and the streets were filled with men wearing greasy canvas clothes, and women with their heads covered with shawls.
," We mun mak"aaste,"'slie heard them saying. "It's but little tay aw'll sup to-neet. Aw mewl to 'ave a front seat." . _
They were speaking about the meeting at the Iduitrial Hall. "What shall I do ?." she asked herself. (To be contimiccl.)

div.head: (copyr,g,.) THE TEMPTATION OF DUNCAN RUTLAND.
div.p: (copyr,g,.) THE TEMPTATION OF DUNCAN RUTLAND.
BY JOSEPH HOCKING,
Author of "The Birthright," "Mistress Nancy Molesworth," "All Men are Liars," "The Story of Andrew Fairfax," Sm.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: Alizon eville, who belongs to an old Roman Catholic family, pays, for curiosity's sake, a secret visit to Tudor Chapel, the Nonconformist place of worship at Lynford. She hears the new minister, Duncan Rutland, and by chance is thrown across his path The virility of his Protestantism makes her half dislike him. She fears he will do much harm among the Catholic population in unsettling their beliefs. Events so arrange themselves that at her instigation Father Sheen; her confessor, agrees to meet Duncan tor a public debate ibtint Roman Catholicism.
CHAPTER V.
A TOURNAMENT OF THE, NINETEENTH CENTURY.

The great audience • gathered at the Industrial Hall was mostly comprised of Nonconformists and Catholics. A good sprinkling of Churchmen we present, but as their position was largely tha', a compromise between the church of ancient cere- monial on the one hand, and the unflinching Protestantism on the other, they did not feel inclined to take ,any prominent part. Besides, some of them naturally felt slightly annoyed that a young Free Churchman should monopolise so much of the attention of the people. When Father Sheen entered there was a great buzz of excitement. His supporters shouted vociferously and gave him every encouragement in their power. The old man looked pale and liaggard, but resolute. Now that the fight had practically commenced he felt far less rear than he had through the past few weeks when preparing to meet his opponent. • There could be no doubt that he was very anxious, but deadly in earnest. He felt himself to le a champion of the truth and was bold accordingly. Moreover, the books he had been reading sustained his courage. He felt sure he had a strong case, and that, how- ever clever Duncan might be, his facts could not be shaken. He nodded to Lady Neville and Alizon, and smiled sadly but confidently when the young girl looked affectionately towards him. On the platform were two tables, on each of jvhich was a large pile of books. "There's a rare lot of dry stuff in yon," said one man to another, who sat close to the platform. "Yi, us 'eads 'll be jammed fall o learnin' afore they've done to-neet. What time is 't? "It wants be three minutes the aaf aar." "Well, th"oud un's 'ere 't ony rooid." "Yi," said an enthusiastic Catholic, who sat close by, "oo's noan afeard. It'll be young 'un as 'll back aat if onybody does." "Aye, but ther'll be no backin' eat to-neet." _ _

As if in confirmation of Ks words several more people took their place on the platform, followed by Duncan. There was a great shout when he came, and a good deal of hissing. "Thee shell be feear play 't ony rooid," said men to each other all over the hall, as they heard the hissing. Duncan was pale to the lips as he took his seat. He was a young man, and this was his first public ordeal. lie had enjoyed the debates at college, but on those occasions there was not an excited throng listening to his words, nor reporters present to take down every word he said. He looked over the audience and saw hundreds of kindly faces and some scowling ones. But he was not afraid. Every nerve was strung to full tension, and his heart beat more quickly than was its wont. The young man had no idea of fear, however. His brain was clear, and every sense Was alert. cip While the hubbub subsided lie looked around the platform and noted the face of Father Sheen. He recognised Lady Neville, too, but that lady took no notice of him. When his eyes rested on Alizon, however, she was looking towards him.- The moment their ,eyes met, shd turned away frau.. him with a smile that was almost contemptuous. Evidently she felt very bitterly towards the man who would attack her faith. - At length the chairman arose, and in a few words stated the conditions of the debate. He had them written down in order to prevent mistakes. Each speaker was, to be allowed half an hour, and the meeting was to last three hours. Thus each man would make three speeches. Having made this plain, the chairman said he had only a word more to say before calling on Father Sheen who was to speak first. It was simply that he expected fair play on the part of the audience. No speaker should be interrupted by his hearers, and the arrangements of the meeting must be carried out decently and in order. "We are met i' Lancashire," said the chairman, "where men like to spaik their mind. On the one hand is a man who has been in the taan for mony a year; I'm sure you'll give him a fair hearing." At this there was general applause. "On the other, is a young man, a stranger to us. Many on us know next to nowt abaat him. But he's the minister of Tudor Chapel, and because we believe in fair play, we'll give him a fair hearing, too."

Again the applause seethed general. "That's all, said the chairman. "I now call upon Father Sheen to open the question as to Whether the Reformation and the consequent growth of Protestantism was a necessity ? ' " There was a great shout as Father Sheen rose to speak, while Duncan noticed that Alizon Neville clapped her hands most enthusiastically. There was a look of eager confidence in her eyes. Father Sheen was an Irishman. He had lived long enough away from his native country to lose some of the brogue for which Ireland is famous, but he had not lost the homely eloquence so com- mon to the Celt. Moreover, after he had uttered a few words and heard the wild cheering of his 'supporters his fear forsook him. He had no notes, and he spoke with perfect ease and fluency. After awhile, too, he allowed the Irish gift of humour to manifest itself, while occa- sionally he spoke with fervour and passion. He spoke of what the Church had done—what it was to the people. Ile described it as a refuge for the weary, a home for the homeless, and the shadow of a great rock in a weary land. He told the audience of its ideals, of its outlook, its unity. Then he described the Reformation, the disunion, the enmity, the hatred, the wars that followed; how families were disunited, how faith was wrecked, and how nations were led to engage in ghastly and bloody wars, "This," he cried, as he saw the hand of the clock pointing to the minute when he was supposed to stop, "this is what the Reformation has meant to Christendom. and I ask you, not as Catholics or Protestants, not even as English people, but as men and women who love righteousness, truth, and purity, was that so-called Reformation a necessity? Alizon Neville's eyes were full of 'joyful tears as her old Father Confessor sat down. To her he seemed like one of the old saints who were heroes for the truth. To her his arguments seemed unanswerable, and she rejoiced with great joy as, in the eye of faith and imagination, she saw thousands in this Puritan town coming back to the Church under whose wings she had been sheltered. Duncan had been jotting down a few notes while the priest was speaking, he had also opened many of the books heft/re him, and marked certain passages. "Old Sheen hey' given 'im a fair 'ard nut to crack," said some of the audience. "Aye, and e'll nOan crack it," replied others. "Yi, but he will," said old Matthy Bray, "yo'll see. Let 'im geet on his feet and ~.he'll mak' mincemait on 'im."

When Duncan rose there was a dead silence. The excitement was too great for cheering. Even his most earnest admirers feared for him. Their confidence, however, was somewhat assured when they saw how perfectly composed he was. He had intended, he said, to have given an address which he had prepared, but he should, perhaps, best serve the interests of truth by traversing the statements of Father Sheen, whose speech resolved itself into three parts. First, there was his picture of the Church before till' Reformation. Then there was the fact of the Reformation, and afterwards, the result of that movement.

Dealing with the first point he asked whether the picture of the Church drawn by Father Sheen was a true picture. If it were, then the Reformers were enemies of the truth and of God. But was it? He then sketched the true state of the Church. He chewed how it had been stripped of faith, of purity, of common decency. He proved from the writings of even Catholic historians that the nriests

div.head: RAILWAY EXTENSIONS AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: RAILWAY EXTENSIONS AT WARRINGTON.

A scene of great activity prevails at the present ' time in the vicinity of Walton Arches. The rural Itspect has been somewhat changed by the erection 'of huge cranes, engine and boiler sheds, piles of red and blue bricks and other building material. In fact it is slightly reminiscent of the days when the Canal was in course of construction. An 'Examiner " reporter went to make inquiries as to What it all meant. He found upon the scene a ' zepresentative of Messrs. Heenan and Froude, of lianeheeter and Birmingham, the well-known con- tractors who informed him that the firm had secured the contract from the London and North-Westernl Railwfty Company to erect a bridge acro,s the Mer-1 86Y near Watton Arches, exactly similar o the one erected by the Manchester Ship Canal Company at this point for the Railway Company. The new bridge is to be erected alongside it, and is part of a treat scheme of railway ext.nsion which is. to be imaiediately proceeded with in this district The main line of the North-Western system,as most tf our readers are aware, crosses the Mersey at 'Talton Arches by means of the handsome bridge Which was erected by the Ship Canal Company and Which provides accommodation for a double set of rails. Within recent years the need has been Severely felt for a wider roadway and it is not. an nnusual occurrence to see trains, and especially goods trains, tied up at Walton for a considerable length of time waiting for the main lino to be Cleared. An extensive widening of the main line leading from Warrington iato Cheshire has now 11een decided upon, hence the necessity of a new °ridge alongside the present one. It will be of the 7,82ne design, and in fact, an exact replica of the ...s4ge now being used. No fewer than 100 men • u Present busily engaged on the work. Exca• ationa to a death of thirty feet have been made tor the crete foundations which are laid in con- on a bed of sandstone rock. The bricksetters started work this week and in the course of twelve nionths it is hoped to complete the work. The Plant already laid down includes an electric lifting Crape which is the first to be used in this district, It is a new invention for lifting heavy weights and bee been foutie of great utility in bridge work. A branch railway line has also been constructed from the London and Nor t h-Western Railway and this Will be a grel.7. convenience to the contractors in the Conveyance of material for the work. Near to the site of the proposed new bridge an interesting experiment is being made by Mr. the contractor for the drede,ine: of the river at Warrington. Plant and machinery have been laid down with the object of pumping the 6hidge teken from the river on to land near the railway. The machinery is not quite in working order bet there seems every probability of the suc- cess of the scheme. No steps have yet been taken by the Railway Company towards making the embankment for the extension scheme but Parliamentary powers have been obtained for the work and it is proposed to einer upon it. immediately. There are also indica- tions that in the near future Bank Quay Station Will be consi•jerably improved if not entirely re- construeted.

CRICKET

Warrington gained a -h;n-d-s-o-m-e victory on Saturday, when thy succeedrd in disposing of New Brighton in somewhat easy :fashion, and tan out victors by 147 runs and 7 wickets in hand. The visitors arrived late, and it was decided to draw stumps at 7.30-

Warrington went to the wickets first, and runs came freely from the opening over, Thewlis and B. Sitcock contributing 27 for the first wicket, when both were dis- mis,el. J. Callon and Dr. Smith then went in and gave the visitors a great deal of trouble. Both Hinde and Jenner, the initial bowlers, were compelled ta retire for Etorspool and Platt. but if anything runs came more tieely, Dr. Smith punishing Platt somewhat severely.

The century was hoisted as the result of 50 minutes' pray, and eventually Dr. Smith completed his 50 with a fine sir hit, the ball travelling on the bowling green. The initial bowlers were again tried with no sum S 3. whilst Eskrigge was tried tor a few overs withexpensive usults: A hearty cheer greeted Callon's hO, but this batsman only added three more, when he failed to secure a short run.

His innings was free from blemish, and included in his score were five fours, the partnership having resulted in tt,e addition of 160 runs. E. A. Connor joined Dr. Smith, and soon emulated his partner by scoring rapidly. Dr. Smith roused the enthusiasm of the speetators by driving Brettragh for four and at the same time completing hi 6 century, whilst immediately after Connor hit a six and four in one over. The second century was sent up, and at 237 the closure was applied, Dr. Smith being not out 116 and E. A. Connor 30.

Dr. Smith's innings was a brilliant display, and after the first few minutes his hitting was exceptionally fins. Both his cu:ting and driving were well timed, and some idea of the rate at which his runs were sewed may be formed from the fact that he was only at the wickets an hour and forty minutes. His chief hits were one six and eighteen fours.

N..?cv Briehton were left with two hours to save the match, arid made, a bad start,losing Horspool in the first over sent down by Thowlis. Hannay experienced a couple of lives, and slow play was the order, neither Jenner nor the visiting captain being tempted to hit out. W. H. Podmore and G Clarke were tried without success, and the first hour's play only resulted in thirty runs being hoisted. Eventually the batsmAn took more lib r.ties., and at 62 Hannay underestimated the abilities of P Amore at cover point, and fell a victim to that player a,t d Hampson's smartness at the wicket.

J. W. Bibby, who had relieved Clarke, now turned the game in favour ef the home side. and Eskrigge, Owen, and Bre:tragh were soon sent back,whilst Dr. Smith got Jeoner leg before and a brilliant catch was responsible tor the dismissal of Tate. Eight wickets were down for 72 runs, and the last pair. Dickns and Platt, offered a stubborn resistance. Connor was tried for a few overs but the players batted confidently and it seemed as if ti-ev would succeed in playing out time. With only five minutes to play, ThewHs was given the ball, and with his fourth delivery he bowled Platt. The spectators showed their appreciation of the triumph by a loud cheer.

div.p: THE FREE CHURCHES.
WANTED, £2OOO.

The July Free Church Chronicle contains an appeal by the National Connell for 2000 to meet the very heavy extra expenses which will be incurred in connection with the Simul- taneous Mission all over the country, in February of next year. The Council is hopeful that it may receive not a few donations of £lOO or £5O and like handsome sums. At the same time it will welcome with great pride and thankfulness the receipt of a multitude of smaller gifts from poorer sympathisers. The Council hopes that the Mission will result in great benefit to all the Churches, and, through them, to our country and the world. But in order that it may be successfully carried out, it is of the utmost importance that the neces- sary preparatory and organising arrangements should not be hampered by lack of funds. Subscriptions should be sent to Mr. Evan Spicer, J.P., 50, Upper Thames-street, London, E.C.
THE REV. It. J. CAMPBELL, B.A.

We are delighted to hear that Mr. Campbell Is making satisfactory progress towards re- covery. He is still an inmate of Shirley Hospital, near Southampton. Doctors, matrons, and nurses have been unceasing in their care, and Mrs. Campbell, who has been staying iu the immediate neighbourhood, is strong in Praise of the devotion shown to her husband. Messages of sympathy from the public have been most numerous, and the ward has been a perfect bower of flowers. It is not expected that Mr. Campbell will be able to take up his work again until September. Very soon it is hoped that he may be removed from Shirley to a quiet country place to recover health and strength. Free Churchmen all over the country have followed his illness with a tender solici- tude.

div.head: FP.IENDS
div.p: THE FP.IENDS

The position of this honourable religious Society has been receiving some attention from the Press lately. It has been stated that the Friends are declining in number, and slowly fading away. This is a mistake. During the last forty years, the membership has increased from 13,844 to 17,153. That is to say the Society is growing more quickly than the popu- lation of th 3 country. Many people, we expect, will be surprised to learn that, of every three new members that the Society receives, only one is a Friend by birth, the other two are Friends by "convincement." The increase of the Society in America is very much more rapid than it has been in England, and, it is needless to add, that in this country the Friends have exerted a beneficent influence, greatly in excess ef their numerical strength.

div.head: ADVICE TO MINISTERS.
div.p: ADVICE TO MINISTERS.

Dr. Robertson Nicoll, of thz) British Weekly, preached to the Methodist New Connexion at Newcastle. After dinner he made an interest- ing speech. Dr. Nicoll is often asked by young ministers to prescribe for them a course of reading. His answer always is "Read the New Testament." This advice, by the acclamation with which it has been received, seems to have struck many people as both novel and sagacious. Probably Dr. Nicoll thinks that ministers de- pend too much on hints and helps and common- t,wies. It is also the case that Dr. Nicoll thinks I..at a real familiarity with the Bible, even as Merstare, is one of the rarest and one of tbe. most valuable of accomplishments. Some time ego he advised everyone to possess a copy in large, clear print, and not to hesitate to mark passages while reading.

div.head: CLEVER PASTORS FOR THE VILLAGES.
div.p: CLEVER PASTORS FOR THE VILLAGES.

An Essex Congregational minister says that when he first came to his charge a neighbour told him that if he would visit his congregation during the week, he might whistle to them on Sunday! An experience of thirty years has taught him that an agricultural congregation is a very difficult congregation to preach to, and. requires a really clever, as well as a good man. Being out of doors much of the week, the tillers of the soil are often rather drowsy in the closer atmosphere of a place of worship, and occasion- ally they fall asleep, but for all that they usually understand the drift of the discourse. It is a sad mistake to suppose that because a minister has a small congregation the work is light. His sermons take as much out of him, and require as much thought and prayer as those preached to the largest congregation. Many village people have to travel a mile or two to church, and they will not go unless they get something that interests and profits them. Many of them are well read in the sermons of Mr. Spurgeon, Mr. Beecher, and other prominent preachers, and are not easy to please.
- REV. JOHN MCNSILL.-DR. PENTECOST.

We understand that the Rev. John McNeill, the well-known Scottish evangelist, has placed himself at the disposal of those who are making arrangements for the Free Church Simultaneous Mission, early next year. Mr. McNeill will conduct the services at the City Temple. We understand that Dr. Pentecost, of Yonkers, New York, who was for a number of years minister of Marylebone Presbyterian Church, will assist in the work to be carried on in that quarter of London. Special attention will be paid during the mission to children. The work for young people during the Glasgow Evange- lists' Campaign was specially fruitful. During six months about twenty meetings were con- ducted simultaneously every evening. The larger number of these were for grown-up people, but eight or ten for boys and girls. Audiences of 1000 and over were the rule, and the meetings more than met the expectations of the evangelists.

div.head: TOTAL ABSTINENCE AMONGST MINISTERS.
div.p: TOTAL ABSTINENCE AMONGST MINISTERS.

Out of 2890 ordained Congregational ministers in England and Wales, 2480 are total abstainers. Twenty years ago only 703 out of 2080 were abstainers. Out of 324 students in the theological colleges from whom returns were obtained, 313 are given as abstainers. In eight colleges, it is stated, there is not a single exception to the rule of abstinence. These figures are the result of diligent research by the Rev. William Mottram. Secretary of the Con- gregational Total Abstinence Society.

div.head: FREE CHURCH UNION IN SCOTLAND.
div.p: FREE CHURCH UNION IN SCOTLAND.

English r eople, as a rule, take little interest in the ecclesiastical events that are transpiring over the Border, and the supreme importance of the approaching Union of the Free Church of Scotland, and the United Presbyterian Church, is in danger of being overlooked. This Union, which takes place at the end of October, means that the !United Free Church, as the new body will be called, starts its career with a membership of nearly half a, million. This makes it, relative to the popula- tion, by far the strongest Free Church com- munity in the United Kingdom. The Wesleyan Methodists and the Congregationalists are the strongest dissenting bodies in England. The United Free Church of Scotland will have a membership almost as large as that of either of these denominations, and Scotland has only one- fifth of the population of England. The Unims places the Established Church of Scotland is very considerable inferiority as regardE membership to the new United Free Church.

WIGAN COTTON OPERATIVES ON STRIKE. The following letter was read trom the Wigan and District Card-room Operatives' and Ring Spinners' Association :—" It will be within your recollection that a short time ago an agitation was comm,neerl for an advance Df ten per cent for males and five per cent for females in wages on tvhalf of the Cotton Ooeratives of South-east Lancashire, which demand after a s!ight show of resistance was conceded. We, the cotton workers of Wigan, have made a similar demand to our csnployrrs, and we have been coolly informed that they cannot see their way to grant it, so that we have no option but to resort to the only weapons we at present possess, namely, a ferike. When 9: e tell you that the average wage of our male workers is £l. per week, and of the females something like 12s for being cooped up in a vitiated atmosphere, which is seldom less than 100 degrees of heat, for 56.?1 hours per week, and when we tell you that we are paid fram 20 to 40 per cent less for our labour than the same class of workers in o'her towns, we think you must admit that we are justified in our demands. We have made many grants to organizations for similar objects in times past, and now that it is our turn to 'face the music,' we hope we shall not appeal to you in vain." div.head: Some Reasons against War.
div.p: Some Reasons against War.

Sir,—At the present time when multitudes of brave men ace being lilted, and greater numlprs maimed for life ; when homes are being darkened by poveity and sorrow, and the burdens of the wople are incre asinv, by leaps aed bounds it may be opportune to raise some se.rious objections to the war which is causing all these terrible cc. !amities. And I think a calm and reverent con- sideration of the character of God, so far as He has been pleased to reveal it to Us, and of His known methods of dealing with mankind will furnish us with some power- ful reasons for adopting this course. Turning to the Sun•iptures. then, we find that the inspired writers all agree in portiaying God as an almighty being of infinite goodness and mercy. One sacs, God is love ; another, that He is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy ; while another tells us that God has no pleasure in the death of the wicked ; and another says He is iongsoffering to us-ward, not willing that any should reit•sh, tul; that all shculd come to repentance. Nor are we dependent on the written word alone for the gracious and beneficent character of the G3d wita whom we have to do; the phenomena of the world around us eepict it in ways so obvious and striking that he that runneth may read. What are the wonderful and beautiful alternations of the seasons,and of day and night, the fruitful fields, the lovely flowers, and woodland melodies but so many demonstrations of the boundless grace and mercy of our Creator and Ruler. Now if all this be admitted surely it is not unreasonable to assume that God cannot be the author and patron of war. To the unbiassed and reflectalg mind it most be inconceivable that an Almighty Being possessed of and constantly manifesting the attributes ascribed to Him in the Bible, and confirmed by the natural world,should deviate from His usual procedure to set up the horrors and carnage of the battlefield. Is there a human parent, so depraved and loFt to feeling in all the world, that he could complacently stand by and see his offspring destroy each other with fiendish cruelty ! Assuredly, no. And can our Father in heaven, the God of love, who is nat willing that any should perish.take pleasure in the mass- ing together of thousands of armed men for mutual destruction; or be pleased with the cries and groans of wounded and dying creatures made in His own image ! Tbe thought that He with whom there is no variableness or shadow of turning could be the God of love and a Moloch at the same time is too impious to b 3 entertained for a moment. _

But the crowning act of our Maker's goodwill to the human race was manifested in the life and death or His Son. We re td that God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, that whosoever beheveth in Him should net perish, but have everlasting life. That Son, Jesus of N,zareth, stood alone as the Saviour of men. Wherever He went the poor and the outcast gathered around Him ; and He fed the hungry, healed the sick, and comforted the weary and heavy laden. And the kernel of His teaching was that men should love God with all their hearts, and their neighbours as themselves, and that this love was to be their ruling srinciple at all times and under all circumstanzes. In His gospel there was no provision made for what our modern christians call just and righteous warm, for all sneer, hatred and strife were absolutely forbidden. And, moreover, anticipating the time when snurious followers would be fcund serving in the armies of the world, He laid it down with divine authoeity that they who take up the sword shall perish by the same weapon. The only sword which the dis- ciples of Jesus may use is the sword of the Spirit—the Word of the living God—which enables them to resist and overcome their spiritual enemies. And then, how touchingly, how pathetically, did Jesus emphasize His maxims in His death. In the words of Isaiah, "He was oppressed.and He was afflicted, yet He opened not His mouth ; Ha is broucht as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so He openeth not His mouth." Nor must it be forgotten that it was not for His friends, but for His enemies that He underwent all this humiliation and suffering. And yet when the Roman soldiers were nailing Him to the cross His compassion for His persecutors and murderers found vent in the prayer," Father forgive them for they know nnt v hat they do." The whole life teaching and death of Jesus. therefore, form such an over- svhclming argument against war, in all its phases that one may well wonder that people bearing His name ars to be found in its ranks, or on its side And when we turn to the first and pure days of the church, before it had been cerrupted and debased by statecraft, we find that the unlawfulness of war was thoroughly understood and admitted. That Christians were found in the Imperial armies even in the first and second centuries cannot he denied. Their number.how. ever, must have been comparatively small ; for Celsus, an epicurean,in a treatise written about A.D. 160, cam plained that the state received no help trona the Christians, either in civil government or war, and that if all men were to follow their example, the Sovereign I would be deserted, and the world would fall into the hands of barbarians. But the con- duct of those seurious disciples who tried the impossible task of serving the Prince of Pace and the powers of darkness at the same time was in no way representative of the mind of the primitive church re- garding war. What that mind was we learn very clearly from Tertullian, the illustrious teacher of the African church, who died about A.D. 220. "You inquire," he writes, " whether a believer may enter the military service, or whether soldiers era to be admitted into the faith, even the rank and file and the subaltern officers, who are not required to take pre in sacrifices or in capital punishments. There is no agreement between the divine and the human sacrament, the standard of Christ and the standard of tha devil, the camp of light and the camp of darkness. How will a Christian man war without a sword, which the Lord has taken away? In disarming Peter He unbelted every soldier." Once more. Although " the Lord is full of compas- sion and mercy ; long suffering,and of great goodness" yet He does sometimes inflict awful punishment upon men when their wickedness passes the bounds of His forbearance. But it is most remarkable that, it is the forces of nature and net human agencies that He uses on those occasions. In the days of Noah the world had beceme so corrupt that God could no longer tolerate it, and the method He used for its destruction was a flood of water so far reaching and overwhelming that only eight peraens survived the catastrophe. Again, how terrible was the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah. Because their cry was treat and their sin very grievous the Lord rained upon them brimstone and fire out of heaven, and overthrew those cities, and all the plain, and all the ihhabitants. And than, does not the apostle Peter teach us that the heavens and the earth which now tsist "are reserved unto fire

against the day of Jadgment and perdition of ungodly I men." There is, however, one case, and so far as I know only one,in which God authorised and empowered one people to destroy and exterminate another. When the wickedness of tie Canaacites had become so enorm• ens that God could no longer bear with it he commis- ' E.ioned the children of Israel to execute His judgment ' upon them. But who will venture to deny God's right to do so, or quote the memorable war led by Joshua in justification of the raiding and killing carried on by professedly Christian people. Until rulers and states- men can, by divine authority, preface their military operations with "Thus saith toe Lord" I fear one must regard their punitive and other expeditions as E 0 many developments of the malevolent spirit which incited to the first murder, and still continues to promote the des- truction of God's creatures.—Yours truly, 23rd June, 1900.

div.head: Doctors Differ, Jury Decide.
div.p: Doctors Differ, Jury Decide.

On Monday afternoon, Mr. J. Dobson, coroner, held an inquest at Runcorn Police Court on the body of Henry Crank, aged 39 years, of Back Brunswick-street, who died on Friday the 22nd inst The deceased bad been employed at Old Quay White Lead Works and had been ailing for a long time. Dr. Rotinson gave a certificate that he had wasted away in consequence of lead poison- ing. Tne Coroner thlreupon ordered a post-mortem examination aud Dr. MacLennan made an autopsy of the boly. Mr H N Linker was present on behalf of the relatives of the deceaFed,and Mr C J Preston (Mr Burton) represented the Lead Company.

Ehza Dunning, wife of James Dunning, Brunswick. street, labourer, sister of the deceased, gave evidence of identification. Deceased was a bach.flor and lived with his mother. He had been ailing two years and had not worked for over six months. Ho went to work at the White Lead Works two years ago. Then he was a strong healthy man. Alter a few months he complained of pain in his stomach and came home" bad.' Dr. Robinson was sent for and told him he had got lead colic. He recovered and returned to work at the same place, but he became ill over six months ago. Be was dismissed for no other reason that she knew than that of being sick. They gave him a character and he got work at the Manure Works of the United Alkali Com- pany, but he was continually taeing off ill and ultima!e;37 cams home and never work.sd again. Dr. Robinson attended him throughout with the exception of the lasf, threa weeks when Dr. McDougall saw him.—Cross- examined by Mr. Graves, inspector of factories, witness said deceased worked on and off at the Manure Works about seven months. —By Mr. Linaker : Deceased told her that he was dismissed from the White Lead Works bs•cause of being iil. By Dr, MacLennan : he did not know whether her brther worked amongst a dusty- material at the White Lead Works.

Dr. MacLennan deposed that he had made a post- mortem examination at neon that day. The body was much macisted and there were no marks of violence. Post-moitem rigidity was well marked. The left leg was considerabiy swollen. There was a slight bluish die- colouration of the gums; and the usual cause of such disco:oaration was working amongst lead. The cause of death was tubercular disease of the lungs.—The Coroner inqeired whether his occupation at the lead works would have the effect of inducing such estate of things.—Dr. MacLennan said the condition of the lungs must have taken some time to develop, and if he were exposed to the inhalation of dust or irritating particles this might have set up some such form of disease.—By Mr. Preston : To have worked in a dusty atmosphere since he left the leap works, would be an exciting cause.—By Mr. Linaker : It was impossible to trace lid in the ss stem by a post mortenz examination and he was unable to say whether his working at the White Lead Works had left lead in the system or not. Ssrne of the appear- ances of the boey were such as would be consistent with lead poisoning. Be had never known plathisis to be set up by lead poisoning. Dr. It thinson called, said he had not been the deceased's regular attendant, but he remembered him having the coin from lead poisoning a long while ago. , From that time he saw no more of the case until April, when he received a notce Ircen the Inspector of Fac- tories drawing his attention to neglecting the law in regard to notitying cases of lead poisoning. He saw the deceased a fortnight ago ; he was in a condition that might result from any number of causes. The general deterioration of the system was quite compatible with an advanced stage of lead poisoning. He would not dispute Dr. MacLennan' conclusion that the immediate cause of death was tuberculosis, but he should think the deterioration of the system by lead poisoning would make him liable to be attacked by tuberculosis. Lead was a most tenacious poison ; once in the system it could never he got rid of. —By Mr. Preston. It was passible the deceased was suffering from chest affections when he went to the lead works ; but be thought not, for according to his remllection he was in vigorous robust health. He thought it probable that the deceased contracted the disease from a relative who died in the house from tuberculosis. His statement on the certificate was that the disease might have originated in lead poisoning.—Dr. McD 'use!l called by Mr. Preston said he was present at the post-mortem examination, and agreed with Dr. MacLennan as to cause of death. It was possible before he went to the lead works ho bad latent tubercle in his , lunge. He had Fenn tee deceased several times since May 20h, and ho was satisfied the deceased was suffer- ing from tubercular disease He had been told that the deceased worked in the open air and not in the works. Even innocuous dust was au exciting eause of disease. After consultation in private the jury returned a verdict that the itnmeeliate cause of death was tuber- cular disease, induced by lead poisoning.

div.head: SUNDAY SCHOOL DEMONSTRATION AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: SUNDAY SCHOOL DEMONSTRA- TION AT EARLESTOWN.

The annual clemonetratien of Sunday Schools attached to the dissenting places of worship in Earlestown and Newton, took place on Saturday under the mest favour- auto circumstances. The early morning was of a very threatening character and one time it was thought that the demonstration would have to be post- poned. Towards ten o'cleck however, the ominous Looking clouds began to break, and a patch of blue sky was the happy harbinger of a fine day. A strong wind was blowing and very soon this together with the sun, which shortly shone in all its brillancy, dispelled frona be roads all traces of the recent rain. It was thought however thet all idea of having the usual field day would be out cf the criestion, but under the influence of the sun and wind tile fields were also rendered availahle, much to the delight of the youngsters. About half past one all the senores began to a,semble on the Market ground, and when all were gathered together, the hymns "Forward ! be our Watchword" and "God bless our Sabbath School " were sung, Mr. W Banton conducting. The Marshals, Messrs. Bramah, Mouutford, Rawlioscn. Smith and Wat- kins took charge of the procession, which moved off the Market place in the following order Earlestown Prize Band ; Primitive Methodists; Congregational, Salvation Army; Baptists ; Welsh, Wes- leyans, Liverpool Farm School band, Earlsstown Wes- leyans. The route was by way of Market-street, Sankev-street, Earle-street,Queetentreet, Railway-st.rect, Faircloug,h-street, to bottom of Cross-lane, back again down Bridge-street, Market-street to the Market ground when the scholars dispersed to their various schools. Thence they proceeded to fields which had been pre- viously engaged, and aftor a short play, all with the exception of the Primitivesaud Ceneregationale returned to their schools for tea. The Primitives proceeded to a field belonging to Mr. Woreley, Nina Arches Farm, and tea was partaken of in the barn. The Congregationa- lists had tea in a field belonging to Mr. W Longton, at Newton. In the other cases, after tea, the scholars enjoyed themselves in the fields in various ways until dusk, prizes being offered for racing, ikc. Bags of nuts, sweets, biscuits and oranges were distributed amongst the children. The Liverpool Farm School Band during the afternoon and evening played an excellent selection of music in the field engaged by the Wesneyans, the lads being in care of Mr. Digweed, the governor. _ _
Mr. J Au . ~tin acted as Sezretary for the demonstra tion.

W HENRY ER legislation iS Our Legislative Dilemma, attempted two schools of opinion are constantly, if nct habitually, active. The first favours drastic measures, in the belief that they are best in the end ; the second will only support moderate bills, and makes much of the danger of legislating in advance of public opinion. Thero. is danger in subnaission to either , school. Several measures, unless the public demands them,are apt to produce reaction and complications; whereas the milder efforts are often useless and have constantly to be amended. The Companies Bill and the Money. lending Bill may be taken as in several respects illustrating what we mean. The first is to be softened to meet objections, though it is art amending bill, and it has been called for because a former measure has been useless, evaded, and hae given rise to many abuses. Something severe wee demanded, and it has not been produced. We ven- ture to predict that in less than twenty years we shall again be found revising company law. ' The second measure is novel, and yet in some respects it is severe. We cannot say whether it will accomplish its object or not, but much must depend upon the administration of the law' under it. The abuses connected with moner lending kave been investigated, and the bill is the outcome of careful consideration. It is thought to be moderate enough to work well. The Workmen's Compensation Act is an illuatration of the moderate kind. It was limited, and it is to he extended before it is half a 'dozen years old. If Liberal opinion had been consulted the Act would have been more comprehensive aud there weold have been less litigation under it. The Licensing Act associated with Lord ABERDARE'S name was regarded as extreme and unworkable at the tire° and opponents came into power to amend it. without venturing to touch its chief features. has proved to be one of the most salutary Acts °lv the century, and the opponents of it have 11° found themselves in the position of its defenderSl and Compelled to resist further changes, though they are widely &manded. The tendency of the ' two political parties is invariably shown in the attitude adopted towards social reforms. The $G.r called moderate reforms are generally the work of the Conservative party, and the original Agriord' tural Holdings Act is a lair sample of its, work. The Liberals had to make it more stringent, and now it is being amended a thitd time, Acts re' specting artisans' clwelluige have had a similar experience. Statesmen have to look well ahead, and if they do not many of their legis' lative efforts soon become out of date. The more comprehensive a reform is, the longer it lasts, sea the better it accomplishes what it was intended t° do. The Cardwell Army scheme and the HarcosrS Death Duties plan are examples of this type se° likely to be challenged. Toe more moderate reform, in short, may be easier to pass, but it is more certain to require ameedeient. The amena. lug legislation of this country is one of the marvel of our party system, becauee it displays a want 01 foresight and a spirit of mere tinkering, like', enough to catch votes, but unlikely to accomplish useful and permanent good. Not only is olit, legislation apt to see-se v between the advance° and the moderate, but our administration is sinli" larly affected. Many Acts are rendered abortive by laxity of central administration, and that ill affected by a theory of politics. Indeed, public opinion must be educated ad quickened, or We neither get sound legislation eor efficient adminir tration. Calling a bid seve-t1 or calling it moder' ate is often a deception, because one can be Veer' ously eaforced, and the othAr can be left, wheh passed, to take care of itsel. An advanced measure, with public opluiozi LLlllitid it, fares bettear than a moderate measure which has only a tePl kind of feeling in its tavour. The career of 01 British Parliament is strewn with the wrecks ° moderate measure: that neir,ipar do good nor. harol• Unless statesmen can look w,3il ahead, as Well 13.4 just in front, they nierely put ;:)od intentions int° Acts that accomplish nothing.
