div.p: ill private households. Trade is largely affected, not only by the withdrawal of labour from certain industries by the effects of taxation. The consumer pays something more than the extra duties ina- Posed on various articles. He is often compelled to contribute exactly double what the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER imposes. In the case of many kinds of tobacco the smoker is doing this at the Present moment. The extra duty on beer may be regarded as having been in some way pushed off by the brewer on the publican, and then pushed 13ta by the publican on the consumer. If the last- named pays no more for his beer he gets an in- ferior article, or lower-priced and inferior articles Enid substitutes are used in its manufacture. With regard to spirits the case is simpler, because the tonsumer has to pay it,undoubtedly,and the quality ought to be the same. The increased Income-tax O n small fixed incomes, especially annuities and Penaions, must compel economies in other ways. The more striking effect is generally an increase of Prices all round. That increase is now steadil going on, under various specious pretexts and some real causes. Labour is less abundant, ex- Ports and imports are interfered with by a rise in freights, and the producer and distributor, having to pay more taxes, naturally endeavour to make inore money out of the unfortunate consumer. Coal has gone up in price, and now gas has followed. Any list of articles that is made out will be found to have risen in price during the past nine. or ten months. Inquiry always leads to the same explan- ation—" It is the war." The logic of the reply is often questionable; of the reality of the effect there can be no doubt. In this country low prices have ruled so long that we are unaccustomed to war prices, and we resent them. But we must Make up our minds to pay them, and the longer the war disturbance lasts the more the process of hardening will extend. The after expenditure on military reorganisation will also have to be met and it cannot be slight. We have entered a ragion of war-like agitation, and it will injure our
trade for some time to come. Low wages cannot

long co-exist with high prices, and so there will be ' Strikes and trade disturbances until matters have adjusted themselves. In fact, war is something that creates rings of ever-widening agitation and expendit•ire.

At frequent intervals there is a black list in the daily papers of soldiers who have died from dis- ease. Casualty lists are insignificant in compari- son, and it is certainly one of the most unsatisfac- tory features of the war that the mortality from disease is so high, much higher even than that due to shot and shell. The last War Office return puts the number of killed in action at: 250 officers and 2,384 men while the deaths from disease are given as: 125 officers and 3,985 men. Dis- ease has accaunted fatally for 1,600 more Inen than all the fighting which has taken Place. In addition no less than 11,255 men have been sent home sick. These facts are striking and compel our attentibn. Why is it that disease is the foe most to be dreaded by the soldier who goes out to fight for his country? Because hospital arrangements are so utterly inadequate seems to be 'the only- possible answer after the . evidence given by Mr. 'Burdett-Contts, M.P., in the "Times." The hon. member's disclosures surpass in horror anything we have read for te, long time, and it is no wonder that they created a sensation among all parties in the House. He tells us of a h3spital within one mile of Bloem- fontein remaining for a Month without beds clattresse9, or nurses, crowded with 250 patients, ninety of them typhoid, where there was only accommodation for fifty. A fortnight later there :era 316 patients, half of them typhoid, in the .te hospital. Still no nurses, beds,or mattresses; fit' not even sufficient- blankets. In some of the toents ten typhoid patients, in all st,lges of the Sickness, were lying so close together that you could not pass between them—` the maa in his crisis' pressed against the man hastening to it. Men lay with their faces covered with flies in _

_ black dusters, too weak to raise -a hand to brush them oft, trying in vain to dislodge them by painful twitching of the features." On a later visit Mr. Burdett-Coutts found the number of patients incre.ased to 496, 300 of them typhoid, and" many lying in three inches of mud left by heavy rain." What excuse can there be for all this? None, but that accommodation was ample when the army was 60,000 strong and the Government forgot to increase it when the strength of the army had swelled to 200,000. Forgetfulness has been a characteristic of those in office during the war, and there will be a heavy reckoning some day or we sadly misjudge the British character.

An increasing number of suitors in the High Courts are preferring their actions to ba tried by Judges without juries. This much is to be said against the judges. Frequently they Are led by the apparent clearness of the evidence to crystal- lise their opinions on it early in the proceedings, and sometimes they are indi3creet enough to show the leaning of their judgment. When that has happened a judge is unconsciously influenced by the thought that to subject himself to the correc- tion of further arguments will involve a confession of error in his earlier view. The judge's training in balancing probabilities, however, more than outweighs the danger, and makes him the main security for the proper administration of the law. As regards criminal trials this holds good even more frequently than in civil actions. During the last few days an Essex jury persi§ted in finding guilty a prisoner whom Mr. Justice Bigham clearly by his summing up regarded as innocent. The judge sentenced the man to ten years' penal ser- vitude, according to the measure of his supposed offence ; but he told the jury he thought they had blundered, and asked them subsequently to help him out of the difficulty by recommending the man to mercy as a correction ofitheir mistake. They accepted the advice, and the judge altered the sentence to nine months' hard labour, and he intends also to bring the matter before the Home Secretary for further revision. Mr. Justice Day last week met with a jury who,in spite of his every effort, also returned a verdict Of guilty. He took the simple course of overriding their view by liberating the man, to come up for judgment if called upon. But these eccentricities of the people sadly mar our old system of inquiry as to fault.

It is to be regretted that in the memorial edition of the works of Mr. G. W. Steevens the first place among the essays should be given to his views on the " New 'Humanitarianism." It was a frank, manly expression against the tendency of the age, but it offers nothing to convince those familiar with the nether side of life that the tendency has yet reached the limit at which it ought to be stopped. Steevens had a contempt for those who held that our prisons by educat;onal processes can be made ref ermative. He declined to believe that crime was largely due to circumstances and en- vironment., and that mon and women could-be made better by an admixture of disagreeable work With softer influences, opening up to them the possible satisfaction of an honest life. All this reveals the brilliant journalist on his weakest side—his tendency to be content with things seen rather than to look below the surface, and back to the curse of heredity. The brute, he apncered to think, must be met on the level by brute force, and could not be shamed into better things by the awakening of a desire to earn the esteem of his fellow men and be decently respectable. Every Prison Governor knows that some natures are hardened, and are no more susceptible to light than an eye when the optic nerve has been des- troyed. But a large number have grown up in euch a way that they would have been offending against their conventiens—and no one likes to do that—if they had net stopped along in careers of crime. Others are the victims of passion, and may be steadied to habits of self-contv4l by the pre- sentation to them of new ambitions, which shall absorb their energies. All that the reformers of

the present day seek is the classification of I criminals, with a wide divergence of treatment; and the Act of Parliament recently passed at the instance of the Home Secretary goes a long way to meet their views.

In the course of a few days the Warrington Electric Lighting Order will come before a corn- mitt 30 oi the House of Lords. Indications are not wanting that a certain amount of opposition will be met with. Locally, opposition was organ- ised by several firms with the object of obtaining protective clauses and as the protection asked for is not of an unreasonable character, an amicable arrangement has been come to so as to avoid a long drawn-out battle in committee. The opposi- tion of the London and North-Western Railway Company is of a more serious nature. Unfor- tunately in days gone by this wealthy company was granted permission to have a level crossing at Wilderspool Causeway and ever since Warrington has paid dearly for this concession in the incom- moding of vehicular traffic and the annoyance and inconvenience of foot passengers. But this is not all. We are now face to face with another diffi- culty owing to this same level crossing. The rail- way company have qn objection to it being traversed by an electric tramway, and how the Corporation's scheme is to be carried through without doing so it is difficult to see. We hope that the scheme will not be wrecked simply to oblige the railway company.

Quietly, but none the less determinedly, the Liberal party in Warrington is preparing for the General Election. No definite information has been vouchsafed the country as to when this im- portant event is likely to take place but whether it comes soon or late we believe the Liberal party, in Warrington will be able to answer the sum- mons to the conflict with a confident cry of "Ready, aye ready." Last week the sub-committee which was appointed some time ago to consider the selection of a Liberal candidate for Warrington was able to con- vey the pleasing information to the General Council of the Association that after inter- viewing Mr. A. H. Crosfield they were unani- mous in submitting his name for approval. The report was considered an eminently satisfactory one, and a resolution asking Mr. A. H. Crosfield to address a meeting of the Council with a view to his selection as candidate was carried with enthusiasm. In this case we have no objection to influencing the decision of the Liberal Council, for we believe that Mr. Arthar H. Crosfield is the best possible Liberal candidate for Warrington. He holds advanced Liberal views on all the important questions of the day, he bears an honoured name in the town, and we believe that he would repre- sent Warrington at Westminster in the highest and truest sense.

The Warrington Board of Guardians seem deter- mined to keep the builders busy. The new infir- mary is not yet out of the builders hands, but the Board has already passed plans for extensions and alterations to the Workhouse buildings,and within the past week, approval has been given to a site upon which it is proposed to erect offices and resi- dence for the relieving officer at Earlestown. Furthermore, a committee is on the look out for a site in Warrington upon which to erect Poor Law Offices. It will therefore be seen that the Guardians have a penchant just now for investing the ratepayers' money in bricks and mortar. The schemes so far as they go are excellent and ought to have been carried into effect years ago. It is even computed that the amount of rent which has been paid by the Guardians ,for Poor Law Offices —which have been far from a credit to the Union—would easily have paid for offices which would now have been the property of the Guardians. But the question arises, whether the present is an opportune time to proceed with these schemes. The poor rate has been increased to provide for the new infirmary and it is probable that a further increase will be necessary if these schemes are proceeded with,owing to the increased cost of maintenance which the infirmary will necessarily entail. Another fact to be considered is the increased cost of building material at the present time, which is practically 25 per cent. higher than a few years ago. These inflated prices will notcontinue for ever,and the Guardians would be well advised in holding over their schemes until the market is more favourable.

Though summer is by no means far advanced, and rain has been fairly plentiful, the Ship Canal has already begun to" talk" and evidences of its presence are apparent at an ever-increasing dis- tance. The hope of dwellers in its vicinity has all along been that it would improve year by year as the various authorities perfected their sewerage schemes and turned out a pure effluent. But sewage schemes, like other schemes. "gang aft agley " and the prospect of the Ship Canal bene- fiting appreciably from pure effluents is remote. Instead of getting better the state of the water worsens, and this year its foulness is communicated to the atmosphere much earlier than usual. For some time past the water has been of an ominous blue-black--an improvement almost on "Stephen's best "—and the odour emanat- ing therefrom is most unpleasant. What it will be like in August one shudders to contemplate, and what the future of Warrington is to be with such putrid streams as the Mersey, Ship Canal, and • Sankey Brook enveloping it and ever worsening, is a prospect equally dismal. Possibly the science and practice of purification may advance and incroase. It is to be hoped so, or the joy of living in this fair land will be reduced to an inappre- ciable minimum.

A Provincial Letter.

That the present war in South Africa will in- volve a terrible legacy in the form of disabled soldiers, widows, ane orphans, goes without saving. It is, therefore, of the highest importance that the various charitable funds available for the relief of Persons who have served or are yet servine in the field, or of the families of such persons, Should be ,istributed with the least waste and to the best advantage. To consider how this could be ancorn- wished a Gev,irnment Committee IVIs anpeintee four months nen, with Lord Justice Collins as Chairman, Lord Northbrook, the Llrd ?,18,T)r of London and others as members, and the committee have now submitted a mot important report. to it are recommendations which, in the interests of the families of the brave men who have risked their lives, it is trusted the Government wilt lose no time in giving effect to. The committee had to take cognisance of several funds, both of a general and a local character, which have been started throughout the country, and it must he very satisfactory to know that they have satisfied themselves there has been little over-lapping, and practicalle no waste whatever of the charitable funds.Tbe report brings out very clearly the necessity of co-operation be- tween those who administer the various funds, and the c orrimittee recommend the representatives of the prineipal local and central funds he called together in London for the parpose of forming a Consultative Council, who shall provide lot the constitution of local committees, both in London and the Provinces to carry out the suevestions contained in the re- port. It is generally felt that the G,,vernment,n3ay now be trusted to act npon the recommendations ,of the eommittee in question. The allowances to soldiers' families should be placed upon eren-r basis, and, ,tR the committee recommend, the relief should in all cases be administered throuee committee:al on the soot. It may well b, thought that no Parliamentary Committee wee needA to discover such a common-sense arrangament as this but the truth is that. it has required three such committees. For the present we have the discomrerting pros- pect of the !MAW, Clines,l puzz!e occupying the prominent position in our morning papers ocennied , for the pmt nine months by the trouble H South Africa. The problem that has to be 9olred is, a most; , painful one, and the statesman who can' p:)W, thus way out of the difficulty will earl tee ;:eititaele and receive the admiration Of ci,u;s,-,11 RropP. Dearth of trustworthy information is the rnes Lu- mediate and pressing difficuPy. If lie rtiyl exp.", ditions could not get past Tientsin tle:y eoule net penetrate to the capital. Tientsin js iverie3.ee by those unacquainted with the topogtelph pee poott- lation of the country as a moderate rivate,ele town, where a little business is done and th eettlatice is comparatively small- But the population of the city alone would make up a number greater thou

div.head: EXAM IN FR3 Fill AY. J UINE 99. 1900.
div.p: THE EXAM IN FR3 Fill AY. J UINE 99. 1900.

that of all the Boers in South Africa. There are crowded into it more than a million of Chinese ; and such calculation should serve to give some idea of the gravity of the situation. During the week the public have strained their ears to catch the faintest sound of the relief of Tientsin and the safety of the force under the British Admiral ; and at length the veil of mystery has to some extent been lifted. But, while we are assured that Tient- sin has been relieved, which removes one cau,e of apprehension, tte news is neither so positive or so satisfactory as regards the position of Admiral Seymour. Moreover, the general situation, instead of becoming more hopeful, is every day growiag more serious and formidable. Prospects of a General Election in the early autumn grow fainter, according to the Press Asso- ciation, as the gravity of the crisis in China increases. It is only what Sllnti members of the tLouse of Commons might he expected to say to the representative of the Association, but leaders of the different political organisations in the provinces would do well not to place implicit faith in what may be mere cabalis-utterances intended to put others off their guard. No one at present knows when the election will come, or whether this year or next, but on the other hand, no one requires to be told that " exPediency " is the password, and that the announcement will probably be made when not expected. In any case, indications have already set in that the present Parliameat is played out and that hon. members are not now attending either at the House or to their duties as their con-, atituents would have them do, and that when the dissolution comes it win at any rate be none too soon for the whole country. Terrible reading is that in the Indian papers as to the famine and cholera As already stated, there are nearly six million persons in receipt; of relief in the famine districts, and the deaths from starvation and cholera are in their number simply appalling. Thera are limits to the purses of the benevolent in this country, of course, but it is a feet that the de— mands of the war funds have diverted attention from the sufferings of our fellow-subjects in the great Dependency, and that while it has been compara- tively easy for the casual contributor to find a place where he could "drop" his shilling for" the abeent- minded beggar," it is not so easy to send a donation to the starving or disease-stricken Hincloo. Post Office people nave responsibities eneuge,truly but thensande of shillings could have been codeeted in the provinces if the local post office were a medium through which these odd centributions could be forwarded. One weuld like to ask our good natured postmasters if it was too late to begin the effsrt now, and, if not, whether they would be willing to interest themselves in the matter. The need for help in India is unhappily increasing She has hitherto helped herself nobly, but cannebe ex- pected to do anything like all that is required. Last week it was suggested in this letter as one means of reducing the chances of railway accidents like the one at Slough, that two men should be placed in each Signal-box inStead of one. This week Mr. W Bramwell Booth comes forward with the question in the " Times" whether in these days of fast travelling, with huge and complicated engines and big loads behind them,two men on such engines are sufficient to guard a train safely to its deetina- tion;whether there ought not to be a third.set apart exclusively, to the business of " look-out " man? While the speed of the train goes on increasing, so does the other traffic, using unfortunately the same metals; and so do the sidings, the junctions, the stations themselves, and with them the signal., Sspecially in the vicinity of oar large towns and great manufacturing centres. The weight and length of the trains are aided to, the steam brake the communication cord and so forth, all represent- ing increased demands upon the presence of mind as well as upon the nerves and strength, of the driver and his mate. Thus the question my be ex- pected to be answered very generally in tbe affirma- tive. Whether the railway companies, with the, enormous demands already made upon them, will regard the matter in the same light, is, of course, another question. From country districts in various parts of the provinces, particularly the south, come more com- plaints even than last year on the part. of farmers unable to hire enough man to assist in housing the crops. About Buckinghanishire some of the farmers declare themselves totally unable to do the work with the hands they have or to procure sufficient assistance. Year by year this phase of agricultural trouble increases, and appears to demenstrate that there is a screw loose somewhere. It will probably be found intermixed with the old problem of wages; for there are hundreds of men in the towns who would be only too glad of employment in the coun- try at this period of the year, if the farmers could or would make some practical suggestion as to how they would he received, housed, and remunerated.

A CHILD SAVED FROM DROWNING.

Edward Jones, Heath-road, Weston, showed that he possessed ample presence of mind, on Saturday morning last, when with a boat hook he hauled tre little daughter (Eleanor) of Mr. Thomas Ellison,2B, Granville-street, out of the Bridgewater Canal. It appeared that a number of little cnildren were playing on the towpath at the back of Mr. Savages abbatoir when the little child was accidentally pushed over into the water by another child named Duckett. Luckily for the infant, however, Jones was passing with a fist at the time and made sensible use of his boat-hook. That the little one was saved from drowning is beyond doubt. As it was, she only got wet through and appeared all right after a change of clothing. • RU CORN COUNTY COURT. div.head: RUNCORN COMPANY'S AFFAIRS
div.p: A RUNCORN COMPANY'S AFFAIRS

In the Chancery Division of the High Court of Justice on Tuesday; Mr Justice Cozaus-Hardy had before him a petition asking. for the compulsory winding-up of the Standard Metabi Recovery Com- pany, Limited, of Runcorn, Cheshire. The peti- tioner was Dir. James Gibbons, brassfounder of St. John's Works, Church-lane, Wolverhampton. Mr Buckmaster said the petitioner was a creditor on a dishonoured bill of exchange given for goods sold and delivered. Execution had been put in for a sum of £34, and had not been paid out. Counsel for the company asked that the petition might be ordered to stand over, as the directors were all away, and probably some scheme would be developed which would obviate the necessity for a winding-up.—Mr Justice Cozens-Hardy refused to allow an adjourn- ment, and made the usual compulsory order with costs.--On a motion to restrain the execution creditor from selling. an interim injunction hp.ving been granted, his lordship made an order for its continuance. Re ordered the men to procure a hand cart, and the defendant was subsequently taken to the station by that means.—Superintendent lieighlev explained that the defendant had been uo at the court fire times previously for unlawful wounding and drunkenness. Under the supervision of Mr J. Wilding, surveyor to the Runcorn Urban District Council, the con- version of Runcorn Common into a resort for pleasure seekers has been going on for some time. The roadways are fairly under way: the drainage, or at least a most important portion of it, hag been effected, and the excavation of the lake is nearing completion. This rapid progress, however, ja to be taken as no criterion for future year,,, but simply as an earnest, that smite day the" Park " will ho an accomplished fact. The conversion will be slow but sure.

There are some p3ople who pretend to uphold the principles or Liberalism and fliunt themselves as broad-minded Liberals, and who would soorn to be told ot the narrowness and instability of their view. Indeed if so told they would look astonished and treat the matter as a joke. "Runcorn's City Fathers" are largely made up of this class, if one is to judge by the policy which has ruled the town in the past and landed it at the end of the 19h century in the insanitary and chaotic condition of things which now exists. There has been no system. no oriier,no thought apparently used in order to make the, town homogenious or healthy. In fact,the share of health the people possess comes more from the natural situation of the town than from any sewerage scheme the "city father." ever invented.

This may seem a sweeping assertion, but one only needs to point to the tinkerinz which has gone on for years past in regard to the ge-verage, in regard to the paving of streets, and especially in regard to back passages. For nearly a ciaart, of a century some properties have been allowed to flaunt insanitation in the broad light of day, and those selected by the local authority for improve- ment seem to have been selected on the " toss- halfpanny system, although some outspoken rate- payers have ventured •to assert that, even in this business" kissing goes by favour." end that some properties have been left so long from the improve- ment scheme because there were friends at Court. It is time the authority quitted this " patch- work" principle and dealt drastically with all properties whether of ancient or modern construeion whose sanitary arrangements, or want of arrangement,are a menace to the public health.

div.head: WIDNES WHEELERS.
div.p: WIDNES WHEELERS.

Several members of the Widnes Wheelers, under the captainship of Mr. Williams, made ttie journey to Liverpool on Thursday. After lunching at a café in the city, the wheelers took the ferry boat to New Brighton. Ilere they repaired to the Tower, where a very enjoyable time was spent, after which the return journey was made. The year-book, which the club has recently issued, has evidently already made its mark in that particular line. Mr R T b: Jones, the honorary secretary, has received a postcard from Mr C A Treater, honorary secretary of the Leipztg Sports Place Germany, intimating that he has heard of the Place, little book, and requesting him to forward one.

div.head: WEDDING AT THE PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: WEDDING AT THE PARISH CHURCH.

A quiet though very pretty wedding took place at Runcorn Parish Church, on Wednesday, when Mr. W Ernest Rowland, son of Captain William Rowland, Eversley, Higher Runcorn, was married to Miss Eva E. Gregory, daughter of Mr. Edward Gre.ory, grocer, Bridge-street, Run- corn. Both parties are well known in the town and/considerable interest was centred in the ceremony. The officiating minister was the Rev EL B Firth, M.A., curate. The bride who wae charmingly attired in a cream silk voile dress, trimmed with lace insertien and chiffin, and wore a hat of white chiffon of becoming style, was given away by her father. She was attended by two bridesmaids, Miss Cissie Stokes, and. Mss Florence Rowland, (sister of the bridegroom). The young ladies were attired in beautiful dresses of turquoise blue voile trimmed with white lace and wore large white picture hats. The bride carried a bouquet of lilies, and the bridesmaids bouquets of dark red roses. The best man was MrFrank Rowland(brother of the bridegroom). A large number of handsome pre- sents was-received by the happy pair. VICTORIA-ROAD WESLEYAN CHURCH, WIDNES.

The anniversary ot the Sunday School attached to the above place of worship was celebrated last Sun- day. The special preacher was the Rev. Albert Clayton, of London. In the morning the children, assisted by the choir.rendered the hymns "Children singing," and" At Thy feet, our God and Father." The choir gave an admirable rendition of the anthem "The Lord is in His holy Temple" (Simper). A service was held in the afjernoon when Mr R Cad- wallador Raby, of Manchester, occupied the chair, and delivered an appropriate address. The scholars sang the special items" Up with the anchor," " 0 Master of Compassion," and "Courage, Comrades." The evening's hymns includel "Thanksgiving," "Onward Christian Soldiers." and "Grant us Thy peace." The choir gave a distinctly fine interpreta- tion of Simper's anthem, "Praise the Lord, 0 my soul." Mr FI Evans conducted, and Mr W Stanley ably presided at the organ. The collections realized the very satisfactory sum of £lOl 03 lid.

div.head: DROWNING FATALITIES AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: DROWNING FATALITIES AT WARRINGTON.

At the Police Station, Warrington, OR Thursday morning, Mr S Brighouse, county coroner, conduc- ted an, inquiry respecting the death of Id ward Rotherham, the eight years' old i‘on of Thomas Rotherham, of Dale-street, Sankey Bridges, War- rington, whose body was picked out of the Sankey and St Helens Canal, at. Sankey, at eix o'clock on Wednesday morning.—The first witness called was Tfannah Rotherham, mother of the deceased child who said that when he went out of the house to play she told him not to go away, She did not see him alive again. On the previous night a gent!ernan sent the deceased away from the canal side. and be promised not to go again.—John James Brinksman 10 years of age deposed that be saw the deceased on the canal bank at 530 on Tuesday night and brought him half way towards home. The deceased stlpped to see some persons playing cricket and witness left him there.—John Jackson, boatman at Sankey Bridges, stated that the deceased's cap was found in the canal on the evening of Tuesday and witness commenced to drag the canal. Re found the body at six o'clock on the following morn- ing. A verdict that the deceased was" accidently drowned was returned.

div.p: FRODSHAM.

PARISH COUNCIL.—At a merting of the Frodsham P4rish Council. held in the Court Room, Frort9ham, on Friday evening. div.head: Gospel Hall.
div.p: Gospel Hall.

On Sunday the preacher at the Goseel Flan was Mr. Joseph De.° of Manchester, who illustrated a Gospel address by the story of Abraham ofTerin,, up Isaac(Gen. 22.) Isaac bad been given to Abraham according tn God's toromi,e even though so old Now A brao,am's sole hopes rest in Isaac and it is a severe tea* of his faith when God asks him to give up this son, but Ws flith stood thii. test for he accounted that God W 4,4 quite atoa to rake his son Isaac again frim the dead, and tha, faith was accounted unto him for rightermanes. In this story there is a beautiftf picture of God's wondrous !eve to man in giving his onlv and welt h-lov-d son to he the Lamb of God, who died to atone for the sin of the world.Goci desires net the death of the sinner but rather that they should come to him and live.

div.head: Child's Narrow Escape from Drowning-.
div.p: Child's Narrow Escape from Drowning-.

P.S. Barnett, and P.C. Oyson were P.m duty at Bridge Foot on Tuesday night at eight o'claCk, when they wtre informed that a child had fallen from the wall at Bishop's Wharf into the river Proceeding to the place they saw the child lying in the river bed about two fe.it from the water. Dyson jumped dawn and handed the child to P.S. Barnett, who then, with the assistance of three soldiers, pulled Dyson up. The child—lvy BrDwnridgefsthr,e) daughter of William Henry Brownridge, carter, 29, Mersey-street—appeared to have sustained no in- juries beyond a wound on the right fnreartn, which the officers dressed. On their advice the mother afterwards tonic the child to the Infirmary, where the house surgeon stated that the injury was not serious.

div.head: STRIKE OF DOCK LABOURERS AT
div.p: STRIKE OF DOCK LABOURERS AT
RUNCORN•

div.head: Further Developments.
div.p: Further Developments.

The strike at the Runcorn Docks has, this week taken a more serious turn, and one, too, which will doubtless bring about an early sett'ement. Up to ab,ut noon on Monday, the dispute was very small indeed, and one vvhicti a trifling concession on the pin of the Ship Canal Company might have brought to a conclusion, for

div.head: WHAT THE MEN REQUIRED
div.p: WHAT THE MEN REQUIRED

According to Mr. Ellie Gatley, secretary to the Upper Mersey Watermen's and Porters' Asseciation,is set out as follows ; —"Tne boat Laders, threugh the medium of the association, invited the company to consider the question of an increase of a halfpenny per ten, which, it conceded would have given the mnn an increase of ±1 per ton over the rates paid in 1879. The rates at that time were as follows :—China clay, flints, and felspar 2d per ton ; blue clay and flints (riddled), 20 per ton. But these were reduced to—china clay, flints, and felspar, 111 per ton ; blue clay and flints (riddled) 21 per ton. 'use company, instead of considering the matter, en- gaged men to take the places of the boat-loaders at the p:esAnt rate. All the men then refused to continue working until their claims were considered. 'The men had not demanded an increase, but had asked the com- pany to consider the matter."

div.head: WHAT THE COMPANY OFFERED.
div.p: WHAT THE COMPANY OFFERED.

The Runcorn agent of the c mapany offered the men sd. per hour, but would not take back old men, slim of whom have been over 20 years in the company's employ. The men demand that all must return. The men earn miserable wages—about 174 61 per week, In fact, when for purposes of the Workmen's Compensa- tiGu Act, it is necessary to state actual earning the com- pany estimate them at 15; weekly. The higher rate, which it is alleged, has been earned, is based upon four weeks' earnings during the notters' strike when the boatmen having no cargo from the Potteries, were compelled in order to g-t a crust, to help these loaders to load their boats. and were actually assisted by their families in the work, and so swelled the actual earn.o of the loaders. Tran company will not give these men's earnings four weeks before the potters' strike, say in March. The allegations of the cmpany that they are paying the same rate at Weston Point is not, true. The men are receiving 1/1 to 111 per ton more kr similar work at that place. And, iurther, the Anderton Orin- pany's boats, usually loaded at Runcorn are now being sent to Weston Point, and a.e being loaded at 34-1 per ton.

div.head: HOW THE STRIKE DEVELOPED.
div.p: HOW THE STRIKE DEVELOPED.

Naturally, &paved of tht. raw material necessary to carry on their factoriea, the manufacturers at the Potteries began to c•uff3r, and pressure was brought to bear upon the carrying companies—the principal of which is the Anderzon Company. Last Monday they deciled to employ their oxen boat _people to _ load_ for

them. This was their last resort, for the officials of the And.rton Company had tri. d the r bet 0 bring about an amicable settlement. The ac ion of employing what the strikers call " knob;ticks," however, no sooner bec woe generally known than the whole of the hands" employed at the Runcorn Docks, the L;y-by and Salt Tip, about 400 in number, struck work. The same night they held

A LARGELY ATTENDED MEETING At the Bruncier Guild Hall, under the pr(sidency of Mr. T Rowe, when after some discussion the following resolution was adopted :—" This meeting of the dock and quay port rs of Runcorn,having carefully considered the claims of the boat loa.tera as rubmit-ed by the Association, and afterwards modified so as to secure the rates in operation in 1879, and recogrizing the re- peated efforts which have been put forth to r,ecilre an amicable settlement, sa as to prevent further disloc iton of trade, herby express our sympathy with our fellow members, rt solve to discontinue work, and call upon all tect'ons of workers in the port 'o co-operate with us so as to e :ure humane considgration of the claims of the boat-loaders, and a lasting eettlement based upon justic and ensuring the return of the whole of the men, old an i young alike, to the servim of the company."

div.head: AN INTERESTING INTERVIEW.
div.p: AN INTERESTING INTERVIEW.

On Tuesday evening Mr Bythell (chairman of direc- tors), Mr. Oldfield (superintendent of the Bridgewater Canal), and Mr. Browning (supnrin`eadent of labeur at Mancnester Dacks) visited Runcorn, and had an inter- view with Mr. J. Meadowcroft (the local agent), and Mr Boddington (managing director of the Anderton Carry- ing Cmnpany, Stoke.) The mecting was held at the Bridgewater Reuse, and eccupied a considerable time, but no decNon regarding a settlement of the question was effected. As a result of the interview many large vessels which would in the natural course of things have stoppA at Runcorn have proceedel to Manchester.

IMPORTATION OF LIVERPOOL LABOUR. On Wednesday there was practically no change in the situation. A rumour gained currency in ase early part of the day that the dianato had been smoothes] over, hut inquiry at the headquarters of the Watermen's and Porters' A.ssaciation proved the statement to be without foundation. Later some txcitement was °tined by the fact that the Federation of Liverpool Ship Owners wore sending 50 men from that p'irt to discharge three large grain ships at the lay-by in till Ship Canal and fears , ware entertained that some disturbance might ensue,but the strikers were reqm,sted by the offir;ials of their as- sociatirm not to go near the ricclas, and they loya!ty obeyed. Groups were to be seen about the streets, but most were to be eeon in the large room of the ass iciation herdquarers pole fully playing dominoes ' and reading newspapers. The Liverpool men arrived at Runcorn Lay-By shortly after two o'clock, having made Vie j iurney by steam tug. They immedietely boarded ' the narcpe " Mayfield "which had a carp of 230 tons of wheat left out 04 a total of 3,600 tons. This ship belongs to Me9qrs Shaw Savilleand Company.of London. The men's first wwk was to attack a good square meal which had been provided for them. Arrangements had been made for them to belodcred and fei on board so that there will be no need for them to come in contact with the strikers by going into the town, and the victualling contract has been placed with Mr George Hewitt, shin chandler. Resider the "Mayfield" the men will dis- charge the" Rnbc " belonging to Mr R W Leyland, of Liveronol,which has on bolrd the greater part of a cargo of 3,392 tons oaf wheat, and the steamship " Corennie " of Glasgow, belonging to Messrs Elak.v Bros., of Aberdeen. Wheo this wnrk is finished the men wi4 re'urn to Liverpo-il the ottur h'oping in the dock being left untouched. The men, it is said are being paid ordinary rates, hot of course are being found board and lodgings be the Salo Owners' Federation.
THE CANAL COMPANY "SIT TIGHT"

Our correspondent had an intervi,w with Mr. J. Meadowcroft the local agent hr the Ship Canal Co. who said he could communicate no information officially. The Ship Canal Company, he stated were sure of their position. Tne earnings of the boat loaders as set forth by the men's represen,ativ.as Mr. Meadowcroft declared to be wide of the mark, and said that if the men would woik regularly st,l c.ors`antly, as they could do, they could earn from 27a to 30a a week. There were cmstant complaints of the men staying away from work, and instances were given of men who having only worked three and a half date a sreels had earnel over 17a and 189 a week. Asked if there was any prospect of a speedy settlement of the strike Mr. Meadow- croft said he did no, know. The company had had no cmimunication from the men's representativea ants i was no for to Ship Canal Co n- panv to run af'er them The men had left work without giving the leas', lreimation although they hRd no griev- ance apart from that of the bcat-toaders. The Ship canal Ceimpany r tight," IS they were sure of their ground, hut he could not give any details of the inner workirr's as his lips were Rested. Of course, it was quite frobable the fietmen would join the tt•ikers which wnuld be a serious mattes, hut still it could not affect the Canal Cornpanr's atti'ude. Mr. Gatier, the secrett•rg of the Watrrmen's anti Porters' Association, was afterwards interviewed, and when told of the view taken IoT the Ship Canal Company seemed gica'ly surprised. He stated, howeyer,that Mr. Meadourcroft knew they were always open for negotia- tions. and if that wag all that was neeied to ptye the way for a settlenrnt it was a matter which could be easily remelied. Asked if the flatmen would also he called out Mr. Gatley said there would be a meeting of the Ex-Putive on Thursday, hut what decisior they ou'd arrive at he could not tell. TEJE SETTLEMENT —A SURPRISE.

Late on WednPsday, Mr Old—field superintendent of the Bridgwater Canal, tt..termanhed to the secretary of the Warermen's and Porters' Acanciation offering the boat-loaders an advanno of a farthing Tyr ton instead of 'h i p•qr t-,An asked fr. At a full meetinr, the men held subsequently it was derided to accept this offer, on cindition that the shipping federa- tion men at the tar-hy were taken back to Liverpool Hero a difficulty arsa as these men in turn rocic out- for tVe payment of sufficient money to nom- 11,11Ree them. In faet they wanted buying out." The s.tm mentioned 30. a Mdn. Independent of this slight de,dlork tlte settirment has caused great eatisfac• tin, hut coming in fare rf the interview with the local agent of the Manchester Ship Can't! Company on Wed- nPtOay, jt iq r+rnewhat astonishing.

ThP mq`,r etarvls with the Mancheater Ship 'in al C:rrn,n-,-, who, if Vier' will nay the Federation meq A wreles c4n Fettle. the affair. If they &Minn timperleFeinn will probably keep them until the vessels are elischlr,sed.

Good Templary. A Good Templar s meeting ‘1711.4 held in the Ternmr- ance liafl, Latchford on Monday evening, the Chief Templar (Br, J Brondrett), in the chair. Personal.
At the Liverpool Consistory Court on Tuesday the Rev. Ernest 1. Tsrbuck, vicar of St. Paul's, Warrington,wds admitted a surrogate of the Diocese. New Organ for St.-feter's Church. _ _ _

On Tueoslay,—Chancellor Espin, presidin-g--in the Liverpool Cousistory Court, St. Nicholas's Vestry, granted amongst other applications one made by the Rev. B. Percival, St. Peter'4Warrington,to erect, at a cost of £230, a new organ in piaci of the present one, which is insufficient.

div.head: Accident to a Boy.
div.p: Accident to a Boy.

A boy named Thomas Carrington, of 25, Leonard- street, wee standing near some machinery at Messrs. Naylor's timber works about noon on Tues. d ay, when apiece of wood flew out and struck him in the abdomen. He was taken to the Infirmary for treatment.

div.head: County Court.
div.p: County Court.

A meeting of this court was held before his Honour Judge Gwynne James on Thursday. The cause list was as follows :-120 original plaint sum- monses, nine adjourned summonses,lo default sum- monses 74 original judgment summonses and the adjourned summonses. There were no disputed cases of public interest. _ _ . _ .

div.head: Music in the Park
div.p: Music in the Park

The band of the Ist Volunteer Battalion (P.W.V.) Smith Lancashire Regiment will occupy the band stand to-morrow (Sunday) afternoon. Bandmaster J. T. Richardson will conduct. The following pro- gramme will be rendered :—March: "rhe Elephant," Hulme ; selection, " Webers Mass in G," Newton ; fantasia, "Day of Rest," Newton; selection, "Maritana," Wallace ; fantasia, "Caliph of Bagdad," Boildien ; " GNI save the Queen."

Serious Accident at Bewsey Wire Ropery. A. serious aceideuc occurred at Bewsey-road Wire Ropery on Monday afternoon. It appears that Charles Thomas Rigby (24), who resides at 4, David- street, was placing a belt on a pulley when his clothes caught in the shafting and he was swung round. He was at once taken to the Infirmary and it was found that both his legs had been injured: One was so s4verely crushed that it was necessary to amputate the limb.

The Dispute in the Building Trades. No settlement has yet been arrivea at in the dis- putes affecting the joiners and plasterers of War- rington. On Wednesday evening, the joiners approached the Master Builders' Association with a view to an amicable settlement of their dispute but no satiafectory decision was arrived at and the strike still continues. The humber of men out of work has been reduced owing to some of them find- ing work els4where. A batch of twenty more has been enszazed and will leave the town on Monday. —A number of plasterers have also found work out of town.

div.head: Local Successes.
div.p: Local Successes.

At the recent examinationincO;nection with the Victoria College of Music, London, held in Liver- pool, on June 18 and 19, Miss A Hill. Napier-street, Warrington (pupil of Mr Henry Davies, ps.e.m., Liverpool), passed very successfully first-class with honours for the Associate of the above college,vvhich will enable her to aifis the letters A.V.C,NI., London to her name. Also she will be entitled to wear the mucr-coveted cap and gown of the college. Also the following pupils of Miss A Hill passed very successfully at the above examination. Below are names of pupils and number of marks gained, the maximum bAng 100 :—Miss M Dunhabbin (Moore), 100 marks; Miss L Gleave (Moore), 90 marks; Miss N Shoebridge ( Warriogton), 95 marks; Mr C Rigby (Warrington), 92 marks: Miss LI Hill (Warrington) 90 marks; Miss L Ma vhall (Warrington), 86 marks; Mis 4 L Warburton (Warrington), 85 marks; Miss J Smith (Warrington), 85 marks; all with honours. Miss Hill has received a letter of congratulation upon the success of her pupils from Mr.G.A.Stantons' secretary to the College. In it he says :—" The examiner spoke most highly of , the excellent manner in which you bad prepared your candidates, and the exceptionally high marks they obtained must be very gratifying to you as their teschAr."

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
NEGLECT OF CHILD REN .-A MOTHER SENT TO GAOL.-
SCENE IN COURT.

At the Warrington Police Court on Monday before Mr. F. Monks and other magistrates, Mary Ellen Harrison, 7, Dakin's-yard, was summoned for neglecting her tour cnildren on June 13 h and other dates iii a manner likely to caL;se them urine cessary suffering and injury to health.—Mr. A. Browne pro4ecuted on behalf of.the N.S.P.C.C. and s'ate I that the woman pawned everything she could get hold of. The clothes that the children were now wearing had been takeis out of pawn to enable i hem to come to Court. Defendant's husband seemed to be a very respectable man. He was an under hand at the forge and earned 27s per week. He gave his wife almost every penny of it and they lived in a cotttage in Dakins Court, paying 2s ed per week rent. The house was in a dreadful condi'aen. The beds had nothing OR them, the bed clothes having been pawned. 'fix society had given the woman every opportunity of reforming, but there was not the slightist improvement.—George Thomas Harrison, defendant's husband, said be had complained to the Inspector on a number of occasioes during the last 12 moo ha. He had bought clothing for the children, but as fast as he bought. it, his wife pawned it. The bed cimbes were all pawned and his wife spent the money in drink. He was lying in bed one day last week (he was working nights) and his wife pulled him out of bed and told him to go to work, She threw the baby at him but the baby was not injured. The beds were not fit to lie in as they were so dirty.—lnspector Hackett ale° gave evidence.— Defendant said that if the Bench would give her a trial she would imorove.—The magistrates committed her to gaol for three months.—Defendant on hearing the sent- ence sefelsimed "my GA" and fainted. She was re- moved fr.en the C ,urt by several constables.

div.head: WIFE'S DISGRACEFUL CONDUCT.
div.p: A WIFE'S DISGRACEFUL CONDUCT.

Samuel Ellison, a brick setter in the employ of the Corporation appeared at the 'Warrington Police Court on Tuesday with his head swathed in banda?es and pre- ferred a charge of assault against his wofe Elizabeth. He was accompanied by his daughter who also complained of being illtreated by hetimother. The facts of the ewe as set forth by Mr. Steel who appeared for the com- plainants were that Ills defendant was a very bad character and had had several separations from hr husband. Unfortunately he took her back again last Christmas and she stayed with him until April 2nd. She ' thee went away but before doing so smashed all the windnws in the house. WhiPt her husband was away at 8 o'clock last Saturday even:rig she came to the house. As there was no one in she went away and returned at 11 o'clock. The daughter was standing on the door Ften and lit f snriant told her to go out of the house. The daughter refused to do en and defer.dant struck liar in the tica with her fist and pulled her away. She then seizad her by the throat and thumped her in the fane. Dehnelant's sister and her daughter then canoe on the scene and they assaulted the girl Shnotly afterwards the complainant arrived and his wife deliberately thr w a bottle at him, striking him on the forehead and inflicting a wound 1.1- inches long and an inch deep. Ellison was taken to the infirmary and his wound was dreesed,but he was still under tbe care of the doctor —Defendant who made her 19'h appearance was fined 204 and costa. or 14 days in the first case, and was hound over to keep the peace and ordered to find a surety of £lO or go to gaol for a further 14 days on the second charge.

VIOLENT' PRISONER.—POLICEM AY A S3A.ULTED.—Patrick Purcell, of Pank-street was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bank-street at 5.30 on Saturday afterno ; and also with assaulting P.C. Carter and damaging his uniform to tke extent of is 6d.—P.°. Carter stated tnat at the time in question he was on duty in Buttermarket-street and saw the prisoner being ejected from the "Crown and Sceptre " public-house. When be got into the street he began to act in a disorderly manner and said he could fizist any man in the street. Witness persuaded him to go to his lorlangs in Bank•street, but prisoner immediately returned and tried to force himself into the Crown and Sceptre. Witness too 'r him into custody and he became very violent and threw himself to the ground. He kicked him on the leg below the knee, and d .maged his trousers. P.S. Hollingworth and P.C. Howard came to his assistance, and with great difficulty they took the prisoner to the Pollee Station.—P.S. Hollingworth corroborated. Prisoner had to be haroolduffed and taken to the Police station on a k.ndcast. —Pined 20a, or 14 days imprisonment BRYVITIEM.—Mary Graham. Gibbs Droved the case.—The Chief Constable said the man was a perfect nuisance. He had been invalided home from the front and this was the way in which he was recruiting his health He had been before the court 29 times, his last appearance being on the 18th inst.—Fiaed Ws and costs or 14 days. THEFT OF HALF A SOVEREIGN —James Rimmer, a lad living with his parents at 12, Baxter-street was ordered to receive six strokes of the birch-rod for stealing half a sover- eign from the house of John Marais, of 3, Howard'e-lane, the previous evening. From the opening statement of the Chief Constable it appears that the lad had occasion to take an empty basket to the house of Mrs. Marsh. Immediately after his departure a half sovereign wao missed from a purse which was on the mantel-piece. Mrs. Marsh went to the home of the boy and at first he denied all knowledge of the matter, but subsequently he admitted stealing it. and stated that when he was going home he fell and the half-sovereign slipped from him and was picked up by another boy, who ran away with it. He professed not to know the boy.—ln answer to questions by the Chairman. the boy repeated the story and was told that it was a very lame tale. In ordering him to receive six strokes of the birch, the Chairman said it the pollee could ascertain the person or per- some who bad received the money, steps would be taken to prosecute them for receiving stolen property.

div.head: Newton Petty Sessions
div.p: Newton Petty Sessions
THunsnir—Before Colonel Wood (in the chiir) and Mr W Collingwood.

ASSAULT ON A GIRL.—SaMUeI MOlvneUX. a boy, was summoned for assatiltmg a gill named Catherine Mawley at Burtonwood on the 21sd inst —Complainant stated that she went to a well to fetch som., water in a bucket. De- fendant came up and kicked her. She threw the water over him and he kicked her five times.—Fined in the costs.

TRESPASSING IN SEARCH OF GAME.—ltiOlitrd HURIG3 was summoned tor trespassing on land in the occupation of James Berry at Haydook in search of game on the 19th inst. —He pleaded not guiltv.—Mr Longton prosecuted and said that on the date in question Lord Newton's game keeper WAS I•xaking after the gime on the land of Mr Berry when he saw three dogs belonging to the defendant hunting in thefields and hedges. One of them was a rahbit dog. He found the defendant lying down close to the dogs. Whe..ber he was lying down to escape detection or to have a "li down' as ha afterwards said they din not know. In the meantime the dogs bad been hunting about the fields and hedges for game,. There was game in that district and at this time of the year dogs did a great deal of damage espeoially to the young game which could not escape. —Fined 5s and costs. THEFT FROM A COLL WkGGON —A boy named John Roberts was charged with stealing 14 ihs o' c.1)1. the prop.rtv of R Evans an i Co , from a waggon at'Edge Green eoldery. Golhorne, on the 16th June —William Latham steed that at 8 p m on the date named he saw the defendant standing on the buffers of a waggon taking coal and throwing it on the ground. He afterwards pot it into a nag, carried the bag about c 0 yards and hid it in a hedge. Witness took posses- sion of It and reported the matter.—A fine of 103. was inflicted.

DoMEsTIC TROUW,E3.—Richard Coppal was summoned for persistent cruelty to his wife Emma on the 23rd inst.—He pleaded guilty. —Mr. Riley apreared for the complainant and said that she had also laid information against the defendant for wilful dam ige to her property. He (Mr. Riley) had, however. had a cmference with them and as the man pleaded guilty to the major charge complainant, was prepared to withdraw the others. Defendant had agreed to a separation order and to contribute lOs per av,e't towards ttas maintenance of his wife.—The order was granted.

F AULa o THF. RAILWAY CoMPANY.—Job Thompson Was summoned on fiVb charges of travelling on the London and North-Western Railway without previously mein?: the fare with intent to avoid payment.—Defendant did not appear and his sister-in--'ew stated that he ha i gone away and W 49 not in his right mincl.-51r. Fenna proseceted and said the man was formerly in the employ of the Railway Company and knew the run of the line thron ih this part of the count' very well. Some years ago he left and obtained employment as a traveller for a coill.ry company and held a eantract. The 'contract expired seine time since and defendant had been travelling on the strength of that coatrsct. He was chal!enge I at War- rington with reference to the contract and was told by the collector that it had expired. He, however, said it had not but when asked to produce it be said he had not got it with him. He had done this en other occasions. Inquiries were made and it was found that the contract had expiret. Defendant was informed of this but still persisted in travel- ing without a ticket and he had even done so since the sum- mons was issued. These were deliberate and systematic frands.—lividence was given on two of the charges and a witness in answer to the chairman said the man appeared t,) be in his right min.-I.—Defendant was fined 40s and casts in the two cases combined and was ordered to pay tha costs in the other cases.

CHARGE AND COUNTER-CH *OWE OF MaLta.T.—Robert To!lett, horse driver, Q ieen's Head-yard summoned Mary lilizabeth Lockett, of Church-street for an assault on the sth Ju e.- Complainant stated that he went to Overton between eleven and twelve at night, and as he was returning he saw defendant standing in Church-walk He ran down the walk, and defendant put out her foot and tripped him with the result that he fell and cut his nose —The defendant denied the charge and alleged that complainant committed an act of impropriety. Conflicting evidence was given. The girl had summoned Tollett for assaulting her, asd after hearing both sides the bench dismissed the summons in the floret case and fined Tollett lOs and costs or 14 days' hard labour. A RIFLE RANGE WANTED AT HELSBY.—Jeseph Fred_ sham, jun., was summoned f.ir tiring a gun within a distane • ot fifty feet of the highway at Helsby on the ICth June.— P.C. ISsucroft stated that at 11.3) on Sunday the 10th inst he WAS on duty in Hillside-road, and was suddenly startled by 9 bullet flying through the air, about 7ft above his head. He went and looked in the direeti.o from which it came end found defendant WAS shooting with a rifle in t)se grounds at his house Witness question d him about using the rifle, and he said he was firing at bottles and tin cans in trees. The shots were going over the road, and there were a gOO4 many people about at the time. Defendant would not be more than 13 or 14 yards distant from the road —Defen- dant now said he was firing at. a target on a tree. The die banes had been measured, and it was found th,t it was 63fe. from where he Was et inding to the centre of the road.—ln reply to the Chairman the constable said he had not measured the distersce He had only calculated it to the best of his judgment,—The Bench adjourned the case in order that the police might make a measurement.

CHORAL SOCIETT.--The members of the above society held their annual picnic on Saturday, the ni3CP s,-Pcted this year being the pretty village of Piumbley. near Knutsford, which they reached by bicycle and 'bus. The weather Perfect for such an occa,ian enabled the members to enjoy to the fullest extent the facilities afforded by the pleasant grounds of the Smoker Inn, in the nape of tennis ano similar out-o'-door games. A capital tea having Iron partaken of, the nerroundine district was explored, incluline a visit to the fine old church of Peover and other places cf picturesque and quaint interest. After a full epj)ement of the excur- sion, the perte made their return j .urney, having a most delightful run home, arriving jut in time to obviate the necessity of lighting up. A STREET SCENE. —At Daresbnry Patty Sessians on Tuesday, before Mr W C Jones, in the chair and other magistrareA. Elijah Cunnineton of Warrington, was cherged with being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart at S'ockton Heath on the 18th June. He did not appear, hot was reerelented bc a female friend.— P.C. Tarte said he was on duty at the Police St.tion at Stockton Heath oe the night in question, at 9 15, when he saw the defendant in charge of a horse and cart. He drove the horse between the permanent seat and around the tree and the lamp—a very dangerous pla.ce, as gener ally there were a niimber of people about that particular spot. The defendant palled up near the Mulberry Tree public-house, and had some difficulty in getting out of the cart. At last he fell on the stones in the road. Witness sew that the defendant was drunk, and he as- slated him into the cart, when " seemed to pull him- self together again" and witness allowed him to proceed. He went a share distance, when he ran the cart into the hedge near the Post Office. Witness then took ct arge of the horse and cart and allowed the defendant to proceed home on foot. The animal Rtd vehicle were suhee- quently taken away by the detendant's friends.—The Chairman fined the defendant 53 and costs.

div.head: ASSESSMENT OF PUBLIC
div.p: THE ASSESSMENT OF PUBLIC
HOUSES.
Messrs. Walker and Son's Appeal.

Mr. Justice Grantham and Mr. Justice Phillimore sitting as a Divisional Court of the Queen's Bench, on Tuesday heard the case of Walker and Son y. Brisley (Surveyor of Taxes), which was an appeal by Messrs. Peter Walker and Son, Limited, brewers, Liverpool. against an assessment by the Income Tax Commissioners made for the purpose of in- habited house duty and property tax on a licensed publichouse in Brunswick-road, assessing it at an annual value of £4OO. The house was only assessed to the poor rate a‘; .f.:39o,and the rack rent at which the premises were worth to be let by the year was £2OO. _ _ .

Their lordships held that the poor rata was no guidance as to value. The principle to be adopted was to get at the full value in the ordinary sense of the word, and not in the technical sense that had been given to it. Judgment was given for the Crown, with costs.

div.head: WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH BROKEN INTO.
div.p: WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH BROKEN INTO.
A Bootless Search.

The Parish Church of Warrington was burglari- ously broken into during Thursday night last week The doors were securely fastened about nine o'clock p.m. by the apparitor and everything was then per- fectly safe. On the following morning, however, he found that an entrance had been effected by one of the windows on the south side of the church. Upon closer investigation being made it was discovered that the burglar or burglars had first of all endeav- oured to get into the building by a window in the crypt. Some strong iron bars prevented them from carrying out their purpose and being foiled here,the intruders seem to have tinned their attention to one of the leaded windows on the south side of. the church. The central portion was protected by iron bars but the windows on either side were not so protected, and these offered little resistance to the depredators. Two sections of leaded lights were cut completely out and an easy entrance was then afforded. Sacriligious hands were laid upon almost everything under lock and key within the church. The poor boxes were prized open, but fortunately the money had been collected on the previous day, and there was there- fore nothing to take. A week previously, a thief or thieves were more fortunate for the same boxes were then broken open and the money extracted. On this occasion, however, they made a bootless search. Finding nothing in the poor boxes, an unsuccessful attempt Was made to open the drawer of a table near the organ. Proceeding down the aisle leading to the upper vestry, a box containing books was opened as was also the choir wardrobe, and some of the cassocks were thrown on the floor. The vestry table drawer was broken open but nothing of value was found therein, ann a visit was then paid to the lower vestry. The drawers were opened and a few odd half-pennies taken from a tin box. Two farthings were left, the burglars evidently thinking them beneath their dignity to take. The boxes containing the surplices, coloured stoles and altar linen were upset and their contents strewn about. The clergy wardrobe was similarly treated, The water bottle was made use of for half its contents were drunk. The lavatory on the top of the stair- case leading to the communion was also used and the towel left carelessly about. In the church itself the harmoniiinas were opened. Beyond the damage to the windows little injury was done and nothing is missing. The door at the south side was used as an exit. The police have been communi- cated with and strict inquiries are being made.

div.head: RELIGIOUS LIBERTY AT BURIALS
div.p: RELIGIOUS LIBERTY AT BURIALS
The Dispute between the Revs. J. S. Hughes and F. E. Powell.

Dear Sir,—Were it not for the fact that the average man is quick to judge of the Merits of a controversy by the amount of argument and abvise respectively displayed by the opponents, I might say something concerning the peculiarly vituperative cone of the letters, particularly of the second, you have addressed to me. But brushing personalities aside it will suffice to draw attention to three important questions of religious liberty, Christian courtesy, and jurisprudence which have emerged in the course of our correspondence. 1. With the first I have already sufficiently dealt and your second letter will, I fear, only tend to confirm the opinion very largely held that some, of those who cry loudegt for religious equality aro among the first to exhibit the most agtouishiog intolernce concerning matters they either merely dislike or are not able to understand.

Secondly, haw is it paptibis to gravels, discuss a ques- tion of taste with one who avowedly sees no discourtety in a Roman priest sprinkling' a grave with holy water in a private burial ground, but who under precisely similar circumstances can only see offence, insult, and outrage in 411 English Driest (who has already given assurance of having had no intention or even thought of wound- ing any susceptibilities) presuming to carry (as was done at Mr Gladstone's funeral) th,-, symbol of our common faith to the foot of the grave? Could there possibly be a clearer illustration of the old maxim De gustibus non est clisputandem ?—(there is no disputing about tastes).

Ltstly, if You really think MP gulty of a misdemean- our the magi terial courts are open in which an ardent advocate of religioui liberty may seek the infrction of a penalty upon one who was merely carrying out the behests of his own conscience. Yours truly.
F. E. POWELL.
June 22nd.
The Volunteer Encampment.

The Battalion Oraers for the lst Volunteer Bat- talion South Lancashire Regiment contain the fols lowing notifications:—The Commanding Officer has much pleasure in conveying to the battalion the entire satisfaction of Colonel J Leith Ross, com- manding the Lancashire Volunteerlnfantry Brigade at the smart and soldierly drill. discipline and general conduct of the Battalion while in camp at Conway. The C.O. also wishes to record his thorough appreciation of the strong feeling of pride in their regiment.and sense of duty to their country which made every member of the battalion do his utmost to attend camp for the full period of two weeks this year, for a training which has been of marked benefitsand which has been taken the fullest advantage of by all ranks. The stronger discipline, hard work done in an excellent spirit, greater personal kn)wledge gained by field training and musketry, increased smartness and general soldierly qualities of all ranks produced by the extended training this year will be of lasting goad to the whole battalion, and augurs well for its future wel- fare, and USE, to the nation as a practical fighting regiment,for which object the whole energies of the corps must still, as heretofore, be employed in striv• lag to attain. The hearty co-operation of all ranks in this y9ar's duties, and the fine esprit de corps." shown ii camp, have been a source of great gratifi- cation to the commanding officer, his adjutant, and the' officers of the battalion.

div.head: HAVE YOU A 6 BAD LEG
div.p: HAVE YOU A 6 BAD LEG

Writi wounds that discharge or otherwise, perhap surrounded with inflammation and swollen, that arnen von press your finger on the inflamed part It leaves the im- pression? If so, under the skin you have poison that daes all the remerties you have tried, which, if not extracted, you never can recover, but. go on suffering till death releases von.
