div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS.
General Movement against
De Wet.
CAPE TeWN, .WF.DNESDAY, 4,35 p.m.

A general movement to s.ttla De Wet ',has now begun, and fighting is taking place between Senekal and Winburg. The steps which art, being taken to crush the enemy in that locality gives much satis- faction here.

It is believed that Both % is ashamed to surrender while it remains possible for Do Wet to boast that the Free State forces have not forsaken the field. While De Wet remains in the field Kruger will hold out. The crushing of De Wet will pave the way to an easy Eettlement.
Major Mosley Leigh Down with Enteric.

New has just been received in Mid-Cheshire that Major a Mosley Leigh, who has recently been prg- mated to this rank, and commands the 22nd Cheshire Company Imp erial Yeomanry in South Africa, his been stricsen down by enteric fever, and lies in the Draghoender hospital. M.lj3r Leigh, who is very popular in Cheshire hunting circles, is son-in-law of Mr. Reiss, Unionist candidate for the Crewe Division.

about Orr-Ewing. He had retired from the service some time ago, and had only been married a few years. Thera is only one officer left in th. War wicks now. Major Orr-Ewing killed. Forbes wounded, Charteria and Flower sick, and Pollock left. We have not heAril in toy particulars. I don't know how badly wounded Dr. Dun is, I hope not badly. Oar trooper doetor left hero last night to take charge of the hospital at De,ooender. Mosley Leigh is fairly bad, and is going in to-day. We don't seem to be any nearer marching than when I last wrote, except that we have got our horsss back. Very few of them look better for the change, moat of them worse, but mine is all right as usual. We have just seen from the kopje two Ihera coming to the camp witri a white flag to give themselves up. I stio rid not be sur- prised to see more rebels come in and give up their arms. They must have g,t a good hiding the other day. It is a shame about the abuse of the white lair!. It was very cold at the beginning of the week. Two mornings there was a ho tr frost, but it is warmer again now, thank goodness. Yesterday our section of 23 men got two sscks fall of papers and parcels, b.sides letters. Fletcher got 14 parcels. I don't know what he will do with them. No tobacco hid arrived for me. Yesterday we had a mounted parsde. " marching order' which M 9,11,19 saddles packed with cloaks, blankets, &I. We heard last Hight that Rther s had got into Johannesburg without a shot being fired ; but he will have a harder march into Pretoria, I expect. We hear no war news here, and have to wait for home papers. 'riser@ are telegrams about such things as the relief of Mateking, that is all. It is now Juno. Time has gone quickly, we nave roughed. it as much as it is possible, I think, for three months now, and almost everyone looks better for it. I doa't know what it will be like getting into a bed again. I am quite used to sleeping under a tree now. I wish we had it bit better food, but we cannot expect that. Breakfast MO, coffee without milk, and biscuits k4l per day) ; dinner one p.m. boiled mutton ; tea five p.m. with ino jam three times a week. Of course we buy stuff when we can, which is fiat very oftei-e As lam writing the Australian gun has just felt from Draghoen- der, the 4th section under Sylvanus Reynolds being the guard. There are come rock rabbits on these k-ipjes like brown guinea pigs, the size varying, from a rabbit to a tox. It does seem a pity that Lord Roberts is making it so public about these generals ; thee nave all done euch a lot of hard work. Two more Boers hay just- come in, on foot, to give themselves up, carrying rifl93 and bandoliers.

div.head: Letter from a Warrington Reservist. A Parody on "Poor Cock Robin."
div.p: Letter from a Warrington Reservist. A Parody on "Poor Cock Robin."

The following is an extract from a letter received by the parents of a Warrington reservist serving at the front with the 2nd Battalion Sonth Gloucester Regiment: —"Saunas Post,South Africa, 30-5-1900 Dear parents.— I received the papers all right. You need not send toe any more papers as 111-- sends me the " Examiner " every week. You can send me some tobacco. I have scarcely any news to tell you. A Royal salute was fired at Bloemfontein when the Orange Free State was pro- claimed a British Colony. We have be.n here a nun. h and where we move next I don't know. We are kept very busy making trenches and tieing outpcst duty every other night. We get a few straggling Boers occasion- a ly. They say that they are sick of the war. We have lost a numter of men through disease. We buried be- tween 50 and 60 men at Bloemfontein including my old chum King. I was very sorry for him as we were chums from our enlistment. We are supposed, according to the papers, to be well provided for out here. Well I have been supplied with one piece of soap since I have been cut at this pest to do all my washiog. Laundresses may lock out " when I return to Warrington. We get jam every day now—one pound between four of us. We hsve about 411- biscuits a day. It is enough to turn us sick to see the way our food is cooked. The tea and coffee is only frightened to death and the cooks gamble for tne sugar. We can buy a few things at the following prices :—Bread. llb 9d ; coffee 7d a 111 d tin ; sardines is 6 1 per tin; cheese 2s 6d a Ify; condensed milk is 3d per tin. I will conclude by sending you a parody on" Poor Cock Robin." :
Who killed Oom Paul ? I said General Buller With my little puller, I killed Oom Paul.
CHORUS. All the Boers in the State Were sighing one and all When they heard of the death of Poor Oom Paul.
Who saw him die? I said General Wkite With my searchlight I saw him die.
Who caught his blood ? I said General Freueh With my little trench I caught his blood.
Who will dig his grave? evdd Bacitm Powell With my little trowel I'll dig his grave.
Who will toll the ball? I said John Bull I3ecause I can pull I'll toll the bell.
Who'll be chief mourner 6 I sairl President Steyn B.canses it causes me great pain I'll be chief mourner.
"Having a Quiet Time." Letter from Trooper Broadbent.

Mrs. Broa,dbent,of The Hollies, Latchford,hß.s received the following in a letter from her son, Lane,-Crrp )val J. W. Broadbent, who ia with the Che9hirci `Yeomanry : Knegas Pont, 31st May. You will have seen in the papers lung before von ret this that there was a fight on Tuesday last at Kis, 35 miles from here. The to'- lo wing troops were engaged:—warveickBbire,L a ncashi re, and Suffolk Yeomanry, Igiahrt's Hone, Moan, strrshire Mounted Infantrvond some lirtilry. Major Orr-Ewing. of the Warwick Yeomanry, was killed at the first shot. Soon after the artillery guns opened fire the Boers put up the white flag and two men went out to pick up their major and were both shot dead. Eight wrrlkdlel alto- gether, and twenty wounded. Captain Wengy Jones (Lancasbires) had his ankle broken, Dr. Dan was sho through the calf, Forbes was wounded, and one staff officer, who ham sire, died. I suppose they ',lssas are not heavy, as we took their laager, stores, ammunition, cattle, sheep. and many priloners. When the column reaches here I expect we shall be relieved. I suppose they are still fighting and making this way, as we have just heard the big gun. I expect by the time they get here tbe rebels will be pretty well broken up. I am sorry

div.head: EXAMINEE, FRIDAY, JUNE 29. 1900.
div.p: THE EXAMINEE, FRIDAY, JUNE 29. 1900.
MILITARY NOTES.

Lieut. Colonel Mansel, late of the South Lanca- shire Regiment, has ben appointed to command a battalion of the Royal Northern rleserve Regirneut. He joined the army in 1869, left the South Lanca- shire Regiment in 1894 on promotion to a half piy Lieut. Colon@lcy and afterwards retired from the army joining the reserve of officers. At one time .be did duty with the depot companies at Warring- ton.

Second Lieut. Dudley Hill just appointed to the 3rd battalion South Lancashire Regiment will for the present do duty with the depot of the regiment at Warrington. The details of the Ist battalion South Lancashire Regiment which have of late been located at Brad- ford on Saturday moved to Aldershot and will be attached t.o the 3rd battalion Manchester Regiment, In addition details of the East, Lancashire Regi- ment are also ordered to be attached to the Ch battalion Liverpool Regiment. To-day (Saturday), the Ist Cheshire E.V. under command of Lieutenant Colonel liamilton will take over qaartets at Chatham where the regiment will train until 28th of next month. The let Cheshire A.V. under Colonel Lloyd will train at Aber from 4th to 18th of August, while the lst Warwickshire AA'. will train at Parkgate, Cneshire from sth to 19th August. Second Lieutenant Gape, lately appointed to a commission in the regular service from the 4th bat- talion Liverpool Regiment headquarters at Warring- ton lia4 joined the 2nd Battalion Liverpool Regiment Second Lieutenant Dinnen also transferred from toe militia battalion indicated has also joined the 2nd battalion on appointment to the regular service. Major Richardson who lately retired from the Cheshire Regiment has been appointed to the 4th battalion Royal Northern Counties Reserve Regi- ment.

Second Lieutenants Wood and Taylor have been promoted to the rank of Ciptain in the Ist Cheshire Volunteer Artillery. They were both lately appointed to the regiment. Second Lieutenant Baker of the 4th Battalion Cheshire Regiment, has been formally appointee a' railway staff officer in South Africa. Owing to the ds.ath of Lard Loon, the honorary Colonelcy of the 4th battalion Cheshire 1-te,inaeot ' has become vacant. Deceased had occupied that posi- tion since 1884 and had previously commanded the old 2nd Cheshire Militia for nine years having been appointed its lieutenant-colonel in 1873. Colonel J M Read a former commandant of the battalion,will now, it is understood, be appointed honorary colonel of the 4th Battalion Cheshire Regiment. Colonel Read served for several years in the regular army and reached the rank of captain in the old 13th Light Infantry. He was appointed captain in the old 2nd Cheshire Militia in 1883 and was lieu- tenant colonel in command of the battalion from 1893 to the end of last year.

div.head: RESULT OF THE WAR.
div.p: A RESULT OF THE WAR.
A. LIVERPOOL CYCLE TRADER OPENS IN SOUTH AFRICA. TWO THOUSAND CYCLES TO EE SOLD REGARDLESS OF COST. NO REASONABLE OFFER IS REFUSED.

Messrs. Hardie, Ltd., of Liverpool, Birkenhead. and Southport, having decided to open branches in Soeth Africa, and it therefore being necessary for the manag- ing director, Mr. R. Hardie, to proceed almost imme- diately to the Cape to superintend matters the.re, the Company have resolved to close their depo', at South- port. Consequently they are now disposing of the whole of their Southt:ort stock, regardless of all cost. It includes Rovers, Singers, Osmcnds, R4eighs, Bards, Dragnaflys, Palmers, Ascots, R telaels. & , and all are being sold at a great sacrifice for the sake of clearance. They have, however, decided to k-ep open their Liverpool and Birkenhead shops during the absnc of Mr. Hardie, and are now offering at hitherto unheard of prices, their stock of cycles, which number 1,500. That this sale is a thoroughly genuine one can be easily ascer- tained on comparing the prices now asked by Hardie, Limited, witn the catalogues of the various makers, as it is now the custom of all large cycle firms to publish in their catalogues the net prices of their machines. As an example cc ..;wo of what Hardie, Limited, are deing we quote the following Two hundred Road Racing cycles, made by Palmeri, of Jarrow, the ordinary net price of which is £l3 134. each, are now being offered for £8 17561, fully guaran- teed for twelve months ; als3 a large number of Singer Gents' Modele de Luxe Cycles for £l2 123, and a large assortment of other makes from £5.

An opportunity liki ;Ws may never occur azain, and we would advise all cyclists to call on Mr. Hardie, at the Liverpool shop in Berry-street, for further particu'ars of the sale, which will dose at the end of the pr2sent month.

The article" How Public Schools Honour heir Dead," appeasing in the July" Windsor Magazine," will app,,al to every Englishman at the present moment. Perhaps the most interesting of all the memorials illustrated is the tablet erected In Glenalmond School, to tho memory of Nexaneer Cumine Russell. •• For, till Time shall be no more, there can be no grander deed in every sonse, done by moral soldier—let alone hv a boy just out of school, a mere lad of seventeen, who vet was an officor in the 74th Highlanders, now the -• Highland L;gh, Infantry.' On Monday a girl named Amelia Joynson living in Lawrence-street, Earlestown and employed as a feeder at, Mesnte. McCorquodale and Co.'s Printing Worke. About 30 of the wheelwrights employed at the Viaduct Works, Etrlestewn had a most enjoyable out to Lericaqer on Saturday. Leaving Earle.- town about Fix o'clock, they reached Lancaster about nine o'clock. Snell after arrival they parte)* lof a substantial breakfast at the Queen's Hotel. The weather was beeutifially fine,and after the meal the party-engegel wagnnnettee and drove to Motes- cambo by way of Heyeham. The annual pionic held in cennection with this choir tODIr place on Saturday. The destination of the choir who were accompanied by the Rev J Carson. was Rhyl, erad leaving Newton-le-Willows at 7-25, they reached Rhyl at 10 o'clock. Breakfast was 13,rved at the Gro,venor Hotel at, 10 15 and was heartily enjoyed. Mr Senkey presided, and he was supported by Mr TT J Lengton, solicitor; kit W Appleby, auditor, Manchester; Messrs Peet, Crotechley, Ritchie, Anclerton, Jackson, and Single- ton. The (Jlial-man moved the report and balance sheet he %adopted. Mr Simpson seconded, and the motien was carried unanimously.—Mr H J Longton briefly reviewed the work of the society during the pact year, and congratulated the members upon its success. He urged them to extend their effort., for a society like that had a great scope in Newton-in-Ntakerffeld. —Mr Appleby also spoke.— 'sir Sankey was unanimously elected chairman of the directors on the proposition of Mr. Jackson, seconded by Mr. Crouehley.—Mr, Sankey thanked them for having elected him for the sixteenth time, which he took as a renewed vote of confidence. The Pavilion had been narefullv locked up on Saturday after the team had finished, and it, is surmised that an entry was effec- ted some time on Sundae. The matter has been reported to the police, and it is expected that the recovery of the articles will only be a matter of time.—At the Newton Petty Sessions on Thursday, George William Tipper, a youth, and William 'Roth- well, John .Toseph Skidmore and Edward Thomas Naylor, bye, were charged with stealing four cricket bate. two pairs of betting gloves, one pair of stumping gloves, one wicket keeper's protector and hall, value £2, the property of the Earlestown Primitive Methodist Cricket Club, sometime between 7.15 P.m. on the 23rd inset and 815 p.m. on the 25th inst.—Thee pleaded gnilty,—grnest James White Al ullin., secretary to the club stated that he saw the Articles mentioned safe in a bag in the pavilion at 7.15 on the 23rd insteTle than locked the doer of the pavilion. At 815 on the 25th he went, in and found the place had been ransacked n,nd the articles in question were mis,in2____pareick Glynn, a labourer said he knew the prisoner Tipper. On Sunday the 24. h inet he met him in Houghton-etrent carryine a bat. He Maid lie had found it in a field. Lie Rave it to witnessanl he took it, home and sub- sequeetly handed it over to P.C. Scbofield.—A boy named Carlin, residing at 60, Houghton street, said m echool on the 26th inst.: he was coming home fro and saw Skidmore and Naylor. Skidmore told him they had got, some bate and were going te start a cricket club. He Old Naylor to "fetch the bats out of the house) and Naylor did So. They gave the hats to him to" mind" and he kept them until P C. Sehefield came.—P.C. Schofield said he apprehended the prisoners. When charged they made s!.e.tement admitting the offence. He found the gloves in a hole in the wall behind Rothwell'S house, and another of the articles he found in a ditch.—The Bench decided to fine Tinper 103. and bound the other boys over to come up for judgment when called upon.

div.head: "THE INCREASING PURPOSE."
div.p: "THE INCREASING PURPOSE."

Mr. James Lane Allen's new story. "Tne Increasing Purpose," is just published by Messrs. Macmillan and Co. The book is the study of an individual nature,seen in its period of growth. In Kentucky, at the close of the war, a great University is established, alai a rough farmer lad hears the announcement as a special call to him ; and his parents.ambitious for their son. as Scotch or American peasants are wont to be, rejoice in his determination to fit himself for the Christian ministry. But the new ferment of Darwin's teaching takes this nature, essentialty devout but essentially free, and his own sect casts him out. He goes back to his father and mother who have pinched for him to tell them that he has been expelled from cr.lleze because he does not believe in Gotl ; and he becomes again a day labourer arid a 'stranger in the house of his own folk. But love finds him in his tragic isolation and brings him into per- 'f-ct harmony with the natural courses of life. That is the central idea of the book, which is really a prose poem : man springs like a plant from the soil, fulfilling the law of his nature, or faiing of it, but destined to be what he is; the possible difference being only ono of kindly or stunted growth. David's faith in the "increas- ing purpose" stown by evolution is sincere as the faith ef his father, but different ; be is the charac'eristic nro- duct of his.race and generation just as the soil of Ken- tucky by a natural fitness produces hemp. Hemp pays for David's college eats, and in his disgrace he returns to labour with the hemp, whose growth and handling is so minutely described throughout, that the book may pass for a Georgic of the hemp.

Certainly the wicket was all in favour of the bawler but 1 think if the players instead of indulging in fancy cricket, had hit out, they would have altered the score Husband and Miller, in whom great faith is pinned for a score were early on, dispord of, in fact Hiller's downfall was evidently due to over cautiousness. Crowther played an excellent game and he looked at one time as if he would carry out his bat, but he was unfortunately caught when he had mad 24. The Warrington Tramways Order. It is expected that this order which is promoted by the Warrington Corporation will CO M 9 before a committee of the House of Lords on Monday next. At the presEnt time the only opponent to the order are the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany, all the other petitioners against the bill. hating withdrawn their opposition.

The Proposed Small-Pox Hospital at Great Sankey. A deputation consisting of members of the Great Sankey Parish Council and residents in the district waited upon the members of the Health Committee at the meeting held in the Town Hall, on Wednes- day evening. Mr. Furness introduced the deputa- tion and bud their views before the committee with reference to the proposed erection of a small-pox hospital at Great Sankey. Several other members of the deputation also spoke. Tee views expressed by the deputation were somewhat similar to those ventilated at the Parish Council meeting held a short time ago, The Chairman of the. committee promised that the views of the deputation would he considered.

NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next GENERAL QUARTER I:,ESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY OF CHESTER will be holden at the CASTLE OF CHESTER, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the 2nd day of July next, at half-past eleven o'clock in the forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be ernpannelled. The hearing of all appeals arising within the Hundreds Of &ester), Eddisbury. Nantwich, and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners corn- nlitted from snot) IlLndreds, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Juries for the Chester District most be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 2nd day of July next, at half-past eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE Court will be Adjcurned to the Court Howie, hnutsford, on WEDNESDAY, the 4th day of July next, sit eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when another Grand Jury will be empannelled. LATEST NEWS CHINA. Admiral Seymour Relieved. Failed to Reach Pekin. ••••••••••. Sufferings of the Force. A Reuters Chefoo te:egrarn, dated on Thursday, says Admiral Seymour has been relieved. He failed to establish communication with Pekin. His force suffered greatly. It is now returning to Tientsin. The Russian Colonel, Stoessel, commanding the combined international forces, 10,000 strang, is supposed to be proceeding to Pekin. There is no news from the capital. The Chinese troops before Pekin are estimated to number between 40,000 and 60,000 men. Boxers are swarming in all directions. 62 Killed 312 Wounded.
